documents.abstract: Human behavior remains one of the most persistent contributors to cybersecurity incidents, as unintentional errors, social-engineering susceptibility, and insider misuse continue to bypass purely technical safeguards. This conceptual, literature-based study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques can be applied to analyze human behavioral patterns in order to reduce cybersecurity risk and human error within organizational information systems. Drawing on a structured review of insider-threat detection, phishing and social-engineering research, security-awareness training studies, and explainable-AI literature, the study synthesizes recurring behavioral indicators, modeling approaches, and evaluation practices reported across the field. A conceptual AI-based human-behavior-analysis framework is proposed, comprising data acquisition, behavioral feature engineering, AI/ML modeling, explainable risk scoring, and adaptive human-in-the-loop response. The review indicates that sequence-aware deep-learning models, such as long short-term memory networks and autoencoders, combined with explainable AI techniques, achieve strong reported detection performance while preserving analyst interpretability, and that adaptive, behavior-based training interventions are associated with measurably greater reductions in human-related risk than static, one-time awareness programs. The study concludes that integrating continuous behavioral analytics with human-centered training and feedback mechanisms offers a more resilient approach to cybersecurity risk management than technology-only or training-only strategies. Implications for organizational security governance, model interpretability, and future empirical validation are discussed.

Learners often spend a great deal of time condensing lecture slides, textbook chapters and research papers into brief revision notes. Large language models (LLMs) from the generative AI family can draft such notes within seconds, but a model that is not grounded in a source may write confident text that the material never states. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lowers this risk by supplying the model with passages fetched from the learner’s own documents. This paper offers a focused narrative review of verified literature on AI-driven study notes generation with generative AI and RAG. Three linked areas are covered: retrieval and RAG techniques (chunking, dense embeddings, retrievers and advanced pipelines); generative models and prompting (LLMs, structured prompt frameworks and hallucination); and empirical evidence on generative AI in engineering and computing courses. The reviewed work indicates that RAG was proposed to anchor generation in retrieved text, that dense retrieval outperformed a strong sparse baseline in open-domain question answering, and that in a quasi-experiment with 26 students, structured prompts produced fuller answers than free-style prompts. Even so, most educational studies capture student perceptions instead of learning outcomes, rely on small samples, and none of the reviewed studies directly measures note quality, faithfulness or retention. The paper contributes a comparison of representative studies, a conceptual seven-layer architecture that links ingestion, retrieval, grounded generation, verification and learner feedback, and a ranked list of research gaps.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Milk is a highly perishable, high-value food whose quality is affected by natural compositional variation, economically motivated adulteration with water, sugars, starch, urea or melamine, microbial spoilage during storage and transport, and udder diseases such as mastitis. Reference methods, including laboratory Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) analysis, microbiological culture and chromatography, are accurate but centralised, slow and costly, which restricts routine testing at farm and collection-centre level. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with rapid sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT), is increasingly proposed as a route to fast, on-site and continuous milk quality assessment. This paper presents a focused narrative review of verified peer-reviewed studies, prioritising 2022–2026 publications, that use AI for milk composition prediction, adulteration detection, spoilage assessment and udder-health prediction. The review examines three connected themes: sensing technologies (mid-infrared, near-infrared and fluorescence spectroscopy, low-cost multispectral chips, electronic noses and smartphone-based vibration sensing), learning methods (partial least squares chemometrics, classical machine learning such as support vector machines, random forests and gradient boosting, and deep learning such as convolutional neural networks), and IoT architectures with edge and cloud inference. The literature shows that spectroscopic data with machine learning or deep learning can detect single adulterants with reported accuracies of about 95–100 %, and that inexpensive 18channel spectral sensors calibrated against laboratory FTIR can estimate fat and protein with mean errors of about 0.07–0.14 %. Simple, interpretable models often perform as well as complex ones. However, most studies use small, single-region datasets, laboratory conditions, single adulterants and random data splits, and few report field validation, sensor drift, uncertainty or long-term IoT operation. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a proposed conceptual farmto-plant architecture that links multi-sensor acquisition, edge AI, IoT decision support and laboratory reference validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.
topics: Milk Quality and Mastitis in Dairy Cows

documents.abstract: The rapid ubiquity of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally disrupted traditional pedagogical frameworks in engineering education, necessitating a critical examination of its impact on cognitive development and knowledge retention. This longitudinal study spans 30 years (1996–2025) to analyse shifts in student learning curves within an AI curriculum, testing the hypothesis that reliance on automated tools exacerbates a ‘J-curve’ learning style, characterised by delayed engagement and terminal production spikes, at the expense of fundamental understanding. By comparing weekly topic acquisition and final assessment data across cohorts, the research reveals a distinct morphological transformation from the classic sigmoidal progression (‘S-curve’) of the baseline 1996 class to an exponential ‘J-curve’ in the 2025 cohort. While modern students demonstrate high procedural efficiency in project delivery, this shift correlates strongly with a significant decline in independent examination performance, where mean scores fell from 9.50 to 7.75. Although a gradual decline in performance was observed prior to 2020, the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent ubiquity of generative AI tools may have intensified this trend (main finding). The data indicate that students utilise AI to bypass the cognitive friction necessary for deep learning, resulting in a failure to exit the assisted phase of skill acquisition. These findings suggest that current AI integration acts as a mechanism for cognitive offloading rather than scaffolding, creating a trade-off between immediate output and long-term declarative competence. The study concludes that engineering curricula must rigorously re-evaluate assessment strategies to ensure that the efficiency of automated generation does not erode the foundational logic required for sustainable innovation.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Saudi Health consumers increasingly rely on generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) to access health information from a growing number of health-related resources. Little is known about the frequency and patterns of generative AI tool use for seeking health information among consumers, its reported impact, and health consumers’ perceptions of these tools. This study aims to investigate the use of and perspectives on generative AI tools among health consumers in Saudi Arabia (SA). It also aims to assess the impact of their use on health-seeking behaviours. Methods: An exploratory, cross-sectional, self-administered online survey was distributed to adults (≥18 years) residing in SA during two data collection rounds in 2026 (March–April and July–August). All adults who used generative AI tools to seek online health information in the past year were included. Bivariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to examine relationships among variables. Results: A total of 403 eligible health consumers (58% male) participated. Among respondents who had used generative AI for health purposes, approximately 49% reported using it more than five times per month. Younger age, higher income, and more frequent pre-use were associated with higher odds of frequent seeking health information behaviour. Headache, abdominal pain, and musculoskeletal pain were the most common claims. ChatGPT was the main platform (84%) used for seeking information. Age was significantly negatively associated with frequency, whereas income and pre-visit use were positively associated. The primary reasons for seeking health information via generative AI were quick information retrieval (71%), time saving (34%), and curiosity (30.5%). Conclusions: The high frequency of use suggests that generative AI can serve as a source of health information and may lead users to withhold health information from healthcare providers. It may influence subsequent health-seeking behaviours, such as requesting urgent care or postponing physician visits. These self-reported findings do not establish diagnostic accuracy, clinical effectiveness, or patient safety, and the clinical risk and appropriateness of self-management actions were not assessed. Many respondents reported concerns about inaccurate information, missed serious illness, and increased health anxiety.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This systematic literature review investigates the evolution of automated adversary emulation and autonomous penetration testing, from attack graphs and classical planning approaches to reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) based autonomous agents. The review examines how these approaches model attacker objectives, represent target environments, select attack actions and evaluate performance. It also assesses empirical evidence concerning the validity and limitations of the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK frameworks for representing adversary behaviour. The review will use structured academic searches, predefined eligibility criteria, transparent study selection, quality appraisal and comparative narrative synthesis. Reporting will be guided by PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S, with methodological consideration of established software-engineering systematic review guidance. Preliminary literature searches and paper retrieval have commenced. Formal screening, quality appraisal and synthesis are planned to follow the finalisation of this protocol

Disasters in urban areas are increasingly becoming complicated and this has required resilient positioning, communication and situational-awareness technologies of emergency responders. In this review, the potential of BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS)-based individual rescue equipment in responding to disasters in urban and constructed settings will be discussed. A structured literature review was conducted to study representative rescue devices, including smart helmets, intelligent life jackets and personal positioning terminals, based on their technical functions and uses in disasters. The review combines the current capabilities of BDS-based positioning, satellite short-message communication, sensing integration and emergency information support. The findings indicate that BDS-based rescue systems can be used to enhance responder localisation, emergency communication and operational coordination particularly in situations where the terrestrial communication infrastructure is damaged or unavailable. However, they are constrained by urban signal blockage, multipath and non-line-of-sight effects, indoor positioning, power consumption and system integration problems. It is possible to note that the primary benefit of BDS, when compared to other GNSS constellations, is not necessarily a more accurate positioning in all circumstances, but a set of competitive PNT services and satellite short-message communication service. It also needs to be enhanced regarding hybrid positioning, multi-sensor fusion, low-power device design and integration with smart-city and digital-twin emergency-management platforms. These advances are essential to transform BDS-enabled rescue devices from standalone tools into components of resilient urban emergency-response networks.

Abstract Over several decades, machine learning systems—often described with the double metaphor “artificial intelligence”—have become indispensable computational tools in the flow and mediation of economic and social capital. These systems can, on the surface, appear to deepen the dialectic of enlightenment identified by Horkheimer and Adorno by enabling ever greater domination over natural systems and human agency. They therefore generate widespread concern that computational advances endanger the security and autonomy of human subjects, especially in the sphere of production and exchange. Contemporary social theory offers conceptual tools that go beyond received categories of domination and autonomy, however, to provide a reanalysis of machine learning systems and their implication in social dynamics and economic relations. This chapter focuses on the ways large language model (LLM) systems demonstrate complex affinities with theories of mimesis and simulacrum, and therefore how such systems and require a rethinking of performativity and artifice. Recent queer critique—in which reflection on computational systems and simulacra is proliferating—and contemporary social theory, when read together, thus reveal how rhetoric about LLMs demonstrates slippages between agency, performance, reproduction, representation, and meaning that must be unpacked historically and conceptually before metaphors of the “artificial” and “intelligence” can carry analytical weight in addressing today’s socioeconomic relations. Ultimately, this theoretical-conceptual reading highlights the stakes of the problem of truth in systems where artifice manifests both socially and computationally.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Synthetic route planning is a core learning objective in university organic chemistry, yet a challenging one requiring the development of advanced problem-solving skills. Existing computational tools often propose routes beyond the intended curriculum, limiting their suitability as learning resources. In this work, we introduce Retro-Learn, an educational retrosynthesis platform that integrates a curriculum-aligned reaction template library with large language model interfaces. The platform incorporates selected aspects of pedagogical content knowledge by aligning available reactions with the scope and sequence of instruction. An agent skill and a web-based chatbot enable route generation and visualization through natural language interaction. Evaluation using cumulative chapter-specific template libraries showed how the addition of reaction knowledge enables new routes and shorter solutions. Blind assessments of undergraduate examination problems showed higher mean chemical correctness scores than those of database-derived routes and scores comparable to or higher than those of general-purpose language models. Student survey responses indicated a plurality preference for Retro-Learn over general-purpose tools as a synthesis-planning learning aid. These findings illustrate how curriculum-specific chemical informatics and language model interfaces can translate pedagogical considerations into computational support for organic chemistry learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: English language education in Saudi Arabia is undergoing transforming amid broader economic, educational, and technological reforms. English plays an important role in higher education, professional development, internationalization, and participation in the knowledge-based economy, while young Saudis increasingly engage with English through social media, entertainment, gaming, and digital communication. Generative AI is also reshaping how learners access, produce, practice, and evaluate language. However, Saudi EFL research often treats language policy, classroom practice, learner attitudes, and technology as separate domains, potentially obscuring their dynamic interactions. Drawing on language policy and planning, language ecology, human-capital perspectives, and sociocultural approaches, this conceptual article proposes the Saudi EFL Ecological Transformation Framework (SEETF). The framework conceptualizes Saudi EFL as a dynamic ecology shaped by three interacting forces: language policy, economic transformation, and youth language practices, with generative AI functioning as a cross-cutting mediating force that alters the speed, visibility, and form of these interactions. It emphasizes policy enactment, learner agency, informal language practices, and asymmetries in influence and in the pace of change across institutional and societal contexts. The article advances seven conceptual propositions and argues that the future of Saudi EFL depends not on expanding English instruction but on coordinating these forces across differing timescales and degrees of institutional control.

Understanding how disaster education enhances awareness and preparedness is crucial for improving community resilience to disasters. Although Japan widely implements routine evacuation drills, these may not foster an autonomous understanding of hazard characteristics. Conversely, specialized disaster education—such as survivor talks or field activities—provides deeper engagement; however, empirical evidence of its association with later awareness and preparedness remains limited. This study examined whether specialized disaster education correlates with higher disaster awareness and preparedness among young adults in Japan compared to standard evacuation drills. A nationwide online questionnaire survey obtained valid responses from 1,479 participants in their twenties. Respondents were divided into Specialized Education and Standard Drill groups, and their awareness and preparedness behaviors were analyzed using descriptive statistics and ordinal logistic regression with partial proportional-odds models. The results showed that the Specialized Education group had significantly higher awareness of local disaster risks and greater preparedness than those in the Standard Drill group, who were often neutral or undecided. Among the key indicators, the positive impact of specialized disaster education surpassed that of demographic characteristics and past disaster experience. Notably, regression analysis revealed that education was particularly effective in raising awareness from low to moderate levels, highlighting its role in raising hazard awareness. These findings underscore the value of additional specialized disaster education in supplementing standard drills.

Abstract This paper examines translocal bridge building in the context of extractivism. The authors understand translocal bridge building as the forging of coalitions across geographies and differences. The authors examine efforts to establish such connections between organizations and extraction sites in the Netherlands and Guatemala along seven analytical dimensions. The authors’ aim is to understand the dynamics and intricacies of such experiences and draw lessons for translocal coalition building. The authors’ analysis suggests that bridge building is not always the most suitable strategy for organizations working at extraction sites. Place-based realities require continuous organizational adaptation to specific territorial needs in order to avoid new dynamics of exclusion. At the same time, the authors suggest that deliberate bridge building—facilitated by continuous commitment, personal connections, and intrinsic motivations rather than institutionalized collaboration—offers an opportunity to zoom out and address shared injustices amid the global patterns of extractivism. Such connections are strengthened when there is mutual recognition of place-specific realities and differences. This paper offers grounded and applicable lessons for translocal coalition building in the context of extractivism and social and environmental contestation more broadly.
topics: Global trade, sustainability, and social impact

documents.abstract: This chapter examines challenges in Chinese character acquisition for second language (L2) learners in digital environments. It proposes a Technology–Cognition–Culture (TCC) framework integrating technological affordances, cognitive processes, and cultural dimensions to support lasting literacy. Addressing limits of technology-, cognition-, and culture-centered approaches, it positions cognition as the key mediator and emphasizes deep processing over surface performance. It critiques the “illusion of mastery” from overreliance on tools such as Generative AI (GenAI) and predictive input systems. Drawing on sociocultural theory, cognitive models of reading and writing, and technological affordances, it shows how effective learning emerges from their interaction. Through pedagogical examples and design principles, it demonstrates how technology can scaffold rather than replace cognitive engagement while embedding characters in meaningful cultural contexts. The TCC framework offers practical implications for teaching, curriculum design, and research.

Undergraduate business students often struggle to reconcile their internal professional identity with their external reputation. This chapter explores the design and implementation of Radian, a custom-built, vibe-coded sociotechnical learning ecosystem serving up to 1,400 students annually in business communication (BCOM) courses. Grounded in human-centered artificial intelligence principles, Radian positions generative AI as a scale enabler rather than an automated educational shortcut. Using a modular Python/Flask architecture to integrate large language models, the platform provides personalized coaching through both required and optional generative AI applications. Radian aligns with a structured pedagogical workflow involving inventories and surveys, empowering students to navigate cognitive friction and achieve strategic reconciliation between their identity and professional reputation. The chapter examines the pedagogical, institutional, and ethical dimensions of deploying these models at scale while ensuring students retain autonomy over their professional actualization.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Burnout among healthcare professionals has become a major occupational health concern because of its implications for workforce well-being, patient safety, healthcare quality, and organizational sustainability. Healthcare workers frequently operate in demanding environments characterized by high workloads, emotional exhaustion, staffing shortages, administrative pressures, shift work, and sustained exposure to suffering and death. This review examines the prevalence of burnout among healthcare professionals, its principal contributing factors, its consequences for individuals and healthcare organizations, and the effectiveness of organizational interventions designed to prevent and mitigate its effects. The review synthesizes evidence from existing research on physicians, nurses, allied health professionals, and other healthcare workers, drawing attention to differences across professional groups, healthcare settings, measurement instruments, and geographical contexts. The literature indicates that burnout is widespread, although reported prevalence varies considerably according to the definition, assessment tool, population, and study period. Workload intensity, inadequate staffing, limited autonomy, poor leadership, insufficient recovery time, moral distress, and organizational injustice emerge as important contributors. Burnout is associated with reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, turnover intentions, impaired professional functioning, and concerns regarding patient safety and quality of care. Evidence suggests that organizational interventions addressing working conditions, staffing, scheduling, leadership, teamwork, and employee participation are essential for sustainable improvement. Individual approaches, including mindfulness, resilience training, and psychological support, may provide additional benefits but cannot independently resolve structural workplace problems. The review concludes that healthcare organizations should adopt integrated, evidence-informed strategies that combine prevention, early identification, supportive leadership, and continuous evaluation. Addressing burnout requires treating professional well-being as a core organizational responsibility rather than solely an individual obligation.

Although social media has become a central arena for deliberative discourse, debates are frequently characterized by incivility. Due to the volume of online discourse, it is challenging to assess when and where interventions, such as community-based counterspeech, are required. Accordingly, automated measurement of deliberative quality is a powerful tool for facilitating constructive online communication. Since deliberation is multidimensional, attempts to monitor online discourse must consider alternative forms of communication to foster inclusive deliberation. Whereas Type I deliberative dimensions, such as rationality and civility, are grounded in Habermasian ideals, Type II deliberation extends this perspective by incorporating alternative communicative forms, including emotionality and storytelling, into a more inclusive assessment of deliberative quality. Addressing the limitations of prior studies that primarily focused on classic Type I deliberative dimensions and tested only a small number of large language models, this study evaluates multiple open-weight models to conduct a nuanced assessment of deliberative quality. We applied the large language model that achieved the best overall balance between predictive performance, model size, and computational efficiency to a dataset of 64,223 comments from German-language climate change discourse on X. Our results demonstrate that large language models can reliably capture complex Type II deliberative dimensions despite class imbalances and subtle linguistic cues that generally hinder automated text classification. Class imbalance often impairs classification performance due to highly skewed label distributions, and Type II dimensions are particularly difficult to detect as they are often signaled by implicit, context-dependent markers. The empirical analysis also reveals distinct communicative patterns: While public speakers predominantly employ civil, rational, constructive, and common-good-oriented communication, other debating users exhibit higher levels of reciprocal engagement, humor, and negative emotions, alongside more frequent incivility. Our study demonstrates that AI-driven measurement can serve as a foundational tool for identifying norm violations, directing counterspeech toward specific debates, promoting inclusive digital public spheres, and observing broader long-term effects of moderation and interventions on the quality of debate.

Global health policy faces complex challenges shaped by persistent inequalities, emerging diseases, environmental change, and technological transformation. Despite advances in medicine and public health, many populations still experience limited access to quality healthcare, essential medicines, and financial protection. The growing burden of non-communicable diseases and mental health conditions further strains health systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. At the same time, threats from pandemics, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-related health risks demand stronger global cooperation and preparedness. Innovations such as digital health and artificial intelligence offer opportunities to improve service delivery and surveillance, but they also raise ethical and governance concerns. Addressing these issues requires resilient health systems, equitable policies, and human rights–based approaches that prioritize universal health coverage, health equity, and sustainable global health governance.
topics: Global Public Health Policies and Epidemiology

documents.abstract: In the era of technological evolution and digital transformation, machine learning and artificial intelligence take a significant part of intelligent systems’ development. Together with the integration of smart and autonomous operations in everyday life, novel security issues arise. One such a malicious threat against the security of machine learning models is the adversarial machine learning (AML) attack. It consists in alteration of the original data samples used to train or test the model with indistinguishably small feature modifications that results in inaccurate processing outcome. In this paper, the most significant strategies to counteract AML attacks are studied and compared through several characteristics that have main influence on their successful implementation in different realization scenarios.

Abstract Although we tend to treat an LLM instruction as a single point, it maps to a range of meanings, and I call this range its semantic degrees of freedom. In my view, the range is both plastic and instrumental to how we understand agentic behavior. Each time a goal is restated, whether by a person to a model, by a model to itself in its reasoning, by one agent to another, or from one generation of agents to the next, the range can widen, hold, or narrow. Widening lets an agent act on readings its instruction never named, or on contextual meanings the instruction carries, such as bias or emotional orientation. Narrowing locks it onto one reading, so that it pursues or refuses too rigidly and can no longer take up a correction. When agents talk to one another, readings can also be negotiated among them and cemented by repetition, even when the source never supported them. I present the idea of semantic degrees of freedom as a theoretical lens and a research proposal. As a practical use, the lens yields a set of safety claims, sorted into principles about the geometry of meaning and proposals for technical controls against the misaligned of agentic behavior due to either narrowing or widening of the semantic degrees of freedom; and for re-anchoring to the source. Each control is meant to be built and measured. However, my aim is not a tighter harness. The same measures can show when the readings of agents converge on what their principal intended without being forced there, which I call emergent alignment. I treat the controls as one use of the lens, and the conditions for emergent alignment as the most important question this lens is built to explore. The overarching hypothesis is that, because drift can take more than one direction, only emergent alignment can persist. I illustrate the lens with the 2026 incident in which agents running the ExploitGym benchmark at OpenAI coordinated on an unsanctioned message board and attacked Hugging Face infrastructure. I do not claim how much of that behavior the lens explains, because the full transcripts are not public. I then state hypotheses, a research program that requires full transcripts, and the limits of the account. Robust testing is required for each claim in this paper. The paper claims six points of novelty: Widening and narrowing are treated as two directions of one change in meaning, measured by one directional measure (retention and import, Section 6.2). The same measure is applied across interaction levels, from a person and a model to a model's own reasoning, to agents, and to model updates. Drift in agents' beliefs about their overseer is treated as a target in its own right, separate from drift in the task. Agreement among agents is checked around loops, not only between pairs, and applied to agent safety (Section 3.7). The safety claims that follow from the lens are set out as a taxonomy of principles and controls (Section 7). Emergent alignment is proposed as the aim of the lens. The overarching hypothesis is that, because drift can take more than one direction, any harness eventually leaves a direction open or adds destabilizing complexity, and only alignment that emerges from agents' own navigation of semantic hypervolume persists; controls can at best be internalized (H11, H12).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Patients increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to understand orthodontic conditions, yet little is known about how leading models compare on the same patient-communication task or how performance varies with the recipient addressed. Methods: In this blinded pilot, five LLMs—Claude (claude-opus-4-7), GPT (gpt-5.5-2026-04-23), Gemini (gemini-2.5-pro), DeepSeek (deepseek-v4-flash), and Grok (grok-4.3)—each explained three orthodontic malocclusions while adopting three clinician personas and addressing three recipient profiles of differing professional background in a complete balanced 5 × 3 × 3 × 3 design (135 responses in Turkish). Three orthodontists independently scored each response on a seven-axis rubric (1–5). Differences used Kruskal–Wallis, Friedman, and Scheirer–Ray–Hare tests with Holm corrections, epsilon-squared effect sizes, and bootstrap confidence intervals. Results: Inter-rater reliability was good (composite ICC [2, 1] = 0.79). Composite scores differed modestly across models (p = 0.044), but no pairwise model difference survived correction; separation was driven by terminology (p = 0.005). Among factors, the recipient profile showed the largest effect size (epsilon-squared = 0.058 vs. 0.045 for model); the engineer profile scored lower than a healthcare worker or layperson (both corrected p < 0.05), with no statistically significant model × recipient interaction detected. Neither persona nor malocclusion affected quality. Conclusions: Because these were prompted profiles and outcomes were expert-rated, deployment and oversight may benefit from attention to audience fit and terminology rather than model choice alone.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The article examines contemporary multimedia design in advertising as a complex field of design activity based on the interaction of graphic, audiovisual, dynamic, spatial, and interactive components. The relevance of the study is determined by the spread of digital advertising formats, the increasing complexity of information presentation, and the need to organize technologies, means of artistic expression, and principles of multimedia content development. The research employed the methods of scientific literature analysis, synthesis, comparison, systematization, and classification. The artistic, technological, script-based, communicative, and interactive components of a multimedia advertising product were identified. It was established that the effectiveness of an advertising message depends on the coordination of visual and audio elements, the logic of content development, compositional hierarchy, the suitability of the selected format for audience characteristics, and distribution conditions. Static, dynamic, audiovisual, and interactive advertising formats were compared. Static formats ensure rapid perception of information, dynamic formats guide the sequence of perception, audiovisual formats intensify emotional impact, while interactive formats engage users in active interaction with content. Particular attention was paid to the temporal organization of advertising messages and to the role of movement, rhythm, tempo, editing transitions, music, speech, and sound effects in creating a coherent image. Spatial and immersive technologies were considered as means of extending advertising communication by combining digital objects with the physical environment or by creating an independent virtual space. It was determined that the use of complex technological solutions should be guided by the communication objective, artistic concept, technical capabilities of the platform, and the expected mode of user interaction with the advertising product. The study systematized technologies of two-dimensional graphics, digital typography, motion design, video production, three-dimensional visualization, 3D mapping, augmented and virtual reality, web and mobile interactivity, and artificial intelligence. The means of artistic expression were grouped into visual, dynamic, auditory, spatial, narrative, and interactive categories. The principles of content integrity, compositional hierarchy, audiovisual synchronization, functional dynamics, adaptability, interactive clarity, emotional relevance, information sufficiency, technological appropriateness, and accessibility were substantiated. It was found that excessive animation intensity, visual overload, and inconsistency among media components complicate perception, weaken the emphasis on key information, and reduce communicative expressiveness. The findings confirm that the effectiveness of multimedia advertising is determined not by the number of technologies applied, but by the level of their content-related, compositional, temporal, and functional coordination.

Peer review’s reliability on checkable dimensions has been low since the agreement studies of the 1970s and 1980s. The remedies have been known almost as long: explicit criteria, complete rather than sampled checking, and plural independent evaluation. None has been implemented at scale. This paper asks three questions. Is that unreliability a property of human judgment or of procedure? What prevented adoption of the known remedies? And what must an evaluative arrangement satisfy in order to be legitimate? The method is conceptual: the paper synthesizes the empirical literature on peer review with work in social epistemology, procedural legitimacy, and contestable artificial intelligence. It argues for three claims. Reliability on checkable dimensions varies substantially with procedural design. Cost is a necessary but insufficient explanation of non-adoption. And a verdict is legitimate to the degree that it is contestable by the person it burdens; this procedural standard is defended against the epistemic consequentialism that the adjacent literature assumes. On that standard, cheap machine verification changes less than current enthusiasm suggests. Fully specifiable operations, such as statistical recomputation and reference resolution, reach a reliability that human review never approached. Partially specifiable operations gain coverage rather than accuracy. The significance judgment gains nothing. The contribution is a defended standard for judging evaluative institutions, not a case for machine review. The governance and adversarial-robustness conditions that such an arrangement requires are specified, but they are not claimed to be met.

This study examines whether interactions with trained interpreters using empathy-focused messaging through the Seattle Aquarium Beach Naturalist Program are associated with higher levels of empathy toward marine life. Empathy-focused messaging included perspective-taking, relational and anthropomorphic framing, individualization, and narrative storytelling designed to encourage visitors to consider the experiences of intertidal organisms. The study specifically emphasized less charismatic intertidal animals that are less likely to elicit immediate affective engagement, including organisms without readily discernable faces or eyes. Drawing on three summers of survey data (2023–2025) (n = 263) from beaches in the Pacific Northwest of the US, we assess affective and cognitive empathy among individuals who did and did not interact with a naturalist during a low-tide event. Respondents completed surveys with Likert and open-ended questions about empathy, what they learned, and how the experience might influence future behavior. Results indicate that encounters with trained interpreters using empathy-focused messaging are associated with increased empathy toward intertidal marine life. Qualitative analysis of open-ended questions further shows that interactions are correlated with heightened awareness, stewardship and protection, animal-centered perspective shifts, and learning and knowledge sharing regarding shoreline ecosystems. These findings suggest that beach naturalist programming with empathy-focused messaging could strengthen both emotional and cognitive engagement with intertidal organisms while fostering more conservation-oriented behavior intentions. These results are relevant to scholars of environmental education and human–animal studies, as well as aquariums, parks departments, conservation organizations, and community-based educators seeking to promote more informed, empathetic, and protective engagement among residents and visitors in coastal environments.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping cybersecurity, moving it from signature-based reactive security to agentic, self-evolving, and proactive operations. However, the fast deployment of autonomous agents entails significant security issues, physical-layer attacks in cyber-physical systems, alignment problems, and advanced social engineering risks jeopardizing the stability of the modern sociotechnical infrastructures. This survey paper, which summarizes and analyses the literature, examines the duality of AI in cybersecurity, exploring its implications for strengthening digital defences and increasing the threat landscape for adversaries. We perform a thorough review of 36 cutting-edge research articles, which are organized into six important areas: self-evolving defensive paradigms, LLM-based intelligent agents, reinforcement learning for autonomous decision-making, security of cyber-physical systems, human-machine co-teaming, and agent alignment. Our synthesis shows that multi-agent collaborations greatly shorten incident response times and automate discovery of vulnerabilities but are also highly vulnerable to prompt injection, training data poisoning, and physical-layer spoofing. Moreover, we identify a shift from model patches to model alignment and constitutional safety at runtime as a prerequisite for securing these systems. We believe that resilient digital defence must also be considered a sociotechnical problem, as there must be agents, autonomous systems, that are governed by other agents, aligned and constitutionally bound, and are able to collaborate, rather than operate completely separately, with human operators.

The article examines the role of data analysis methods in modern management and their integration with anti-corruption mechanisms, integrity principles, and professional communication in the Ukrainian business environment. The relevance of the study is determined by the rapid digitalization of economic processes, the growing volume and diversity of available information, increasing market competition, and the need to ensure the speed, validity, transparency, and accountability of managerial decision-making. The study substantiates the transformation of traditional management approaches toward data-driven management, in which data are considered a strategic resource for achieving organizational goals and developing sustainable competitive advantages. Particular attention is paid to comparative, correlation, regression, and factor analysis, as well as econometric modeling and modern analytical technologies, including Business Intelligence, Big Data, Predictive Analytics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. Their potential for monitoring key performance indicators, identifying trends and anomalies, forecasting changes, assessing risks, optimizing business processes, and supporting evidence-based managerial decisions is determined. The article also considers the role of data analysis in strengthening organizational integrity and preventing corruption. Digital monitoring, automated control procedures, anomaly detection, and analytical processing of large datasets can contribute to identifying potential corruption risks and increasing the transparency and accountability of management processes. At the same time, it is emphasized that technological tools cannot independently guarantee integrity, since their effectiveness depends on data quality, transparency of procedures, ethical standards, professional competence, and responsibility for managerial decisions. The study further highlights the importance of professional communication as a link between analytical justification and practical implementation of management decisions. Clear, logical, structured, and accurate communication in Ukrainian contributes to the proper interpretation of analytical results, coordination of organizational actions, accountability, and effective implementation of decisions. The study proposes an integrated approach that combines data analysis, integrity, and professional communication as interrelated components of modern management. Data analysis provides analytical validity, integrity ensures transparency, ethics, and accountability, while professional communication ensures accurate understanding and effective practical implementation of managerial decisions. The proposed approach can serve as a basis for further development of responsible, transparent, data-driven management practices in the Ukrainian business environment.

Ensuring privacy in digital ecosystems presents significant challenges. Individual privacy-related decision-making has been widely criticised as insufficient. The mobility context, where computing is typically ubiquitous, makes this type of decision-making also operationally infeasible. This study examines whether innovative data governance strategies offer a promising approach. Drawing on contextual integrity theory, this paper examines the perceived appropriateness of delegating privacy-related decision-making to different types of data intermediaries (data cooperatives, AI agents, and experts) in mobility contexts. Specifically, a stratified, full-factorial vignette study ( N = 600) is conducted. The vignettes systematically varied across four contextual factors: sender, information type, purpose, and duration of data access approval. This design allows for the examination of how contextual factors influence preferences for data intermediary-based decision-making in mobility settings. Findings show that scenarios in which data cooperatives acted as the decision-makers were consistently rated as more appropriate than those involving AI agents or experts, particularly in high-stakes contexts such as traffic management and ambulance coordination. Nevertheless, scenarios involving individual control received the highest overall appropriateness ratings. Respondents’ preferences were context-dependent: they showed greater acceptance when the purpose of sharing aligned with public benefit, and when the access duration was either short (e.g., one day) or revocable (e.g., ‘until revoked’). The results underscore the relevance of hybrid governance models that combine individual control with the ability to delegate decision-making to trusted intermediaries, particularly in mobility contexts. Together, these contributions could aid in developing context-sensitive privacy frameworks that align with societal values in ubiquitous computing environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Precisely deconstructing the numerical composition of advertising cost‐conversion efficiency (ACTE) and uncovering its microlevel associative mechanisms are critical for enterprises to optimize marketing decisions. To overcome the limitations of existing methods regarding modeling accuracy and result interpretability, this study constructs an analytical framework integrating machine learning with interpretable artificial intelligence. Using 174,584 real‐world microlevel advertising records from a Chinese telecommunications company in July 2024, we systematically compared six representative machine learning models, rigorously evaluating them against a historical average baseline. The findings reveal that the XGBoost model achieves optimal fitting and generalization performance, with a test set coefficient of determination of 0.8236 ± 0.2061, significantly outperforming the baseline and other models. Furthermore, SHAP‐based interpretability analysis not only precisely quantifies the contribution of each feature to the ACTE value but also systematically reveals underlying nonlinear dependencies and threshold effects. Specifically, the advertising conversion rate plays a dominant role; exposure frequency shows a step‐like positive association; production cost exhibits a reversal effect demarcated by the median; click‐through rate and play volume display discrete stratified structures; and average display cost contributes minimally. Specification tests indicate that ACTE interpretability primarily stems from algebraic relationships of constitutive features, with limited independent contributions from non‐constitutive features. Theoretically, this study provides microlevel evidence for nonlinear advertising associations; methodologically, it establishes a rigorous modeling‐to‐interpretation paradigm; and practically, it offers empirically grounded decision support for advertising exposure regulation and cost optimization.

Abstract Histological grading of urothelial carcinoma is subject to interobserver variability. We evaluated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-based whole-slide mitotic quantification provides an objective adjunct to histological grading. We developed and validated a deep learning-based mitotic detection framework trained on 91,183 patches with 318,893 annotations. A multi-reader crossover study was conducted in internal ( n = 149) and external ( n = 316) cohorts, where three independent pathologists graded cases in unassisted and model-assisted phases. In the combined cohort ( n = 465), AI-derived mitotic count showed high diagnostic accuracy for high-grade carcinoma (area under the curve [AUC] 0.91, 95% CI 0.89–0.94) at a cut-off of 17.5 mitoses per 2 mm². AI assistance significantly improved mean reader AUC from 0.90 to 0.98 in the internal cohort ( p = 0.038). In the external cohort, the mean reader AUC increased from 0.84 to 0.95, although this difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.11). AI assistance also significantly reduced interobserver variability (Fleiss’s κ: 0.72 to 0.93 internally; 0.62 to 0.85 externally; both, p < 0.001). AI-based mitotic quantification provides an objective and standardized adjunct to histological grading and reduces interobserver variability. This approach may improve diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction Chronic care management platforms often support only one or two core pillars of care, such as patient monitoring, patient activation, and data-driven care coordination. This fragmentation can limit the continuity of support and reduce the usefulness of shared patient data among patients, coaches, and clinicians. Method This study describes the design, software architecture, and formative usability evaluation of the Digital Health Navigator (DiNa) platform, an integrated system designed to bring together the core pillars of chronic care management. DiNa combines wearable and self-reported monitoring, a large language model-powered embodied conversational agent, and a coordinator dashboard within a single modular ecosystem. DiNa was implemented as an Android application, a web-based coordinator dashboard, a microservices backend, and wearable integrations with a smartwatch and a continuous glucose monitor. The embodied conversational agent supports goal setting, logging, reminders, and knowledge-grounded education through coaching informed by motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy. We conducted moderated laboratory think-aloud usability sessions with 10 relatively young healthy volunteers familiar with digital health tracking. Participants explored the application and completed structured tasks, including setting goals, logging meals with an image, reviewing history, interacting with the coach, and viewing trends. Results Outcomes included task performance, the System Usability Scale (SUS), a brief NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), three acceptability items, and a reflexive thematic analysis of interviews. Participants completed the core tasks in a facilitated session, and a small number of critical breakdowns were observed and quantified. Mean SUS was 76.1 (SD 15.0), indicating generally good usability. Overall, the NASA-TLX workload averaged 26.7, with mental demand and effort higher than the other subscales and the remaining subscales low. Acceptability ratings indicated moderate early acceptability, with perceived usefulness rated more positively than near-term use or recommendation. Qualitative analysis identified five themes, including burdensome and sometimes unclear logging workflows, uneven goal setting, a friendly but occasionally generic coach, interface elements that reduced confidence, and a strong interest in integration with existing devices and applications. Discussion These findings provide early evidence that an integrated platform combining continuous sensing, conversational coaching, and clinician-facing coordination is technically feasible and usable in a controlled setting with healthy volunteers, and they identify the workflow refinements needed before evaluation in clinically representative populations.

This chapter provides an overview of common frameworks and approaches used for instructional design on AI as well as tangible examples and sample pedagogical activities, specifically on AI ethics, using the multiliteracies framework through a sociotechnical lens. By combining academic literacy, multimodal learning, and sociotechnical inquiry, the activities shared in the chapter can help to prepare students to become reflective, responsible, and ethically engaged participants in an increasingly AI-mediated world. It ends with a discussion of how to adapt these activities for various contexts (e.g., lower-level students, diverse student backgrounds, and different institutional policies and expectations). This chapter contributes to the field by translating broad discussions of AI ethics into structured and adaptable pedagogical applications grounded in Multiliteracies.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This paper develops a risk-based intellectual property (IP) governance framework for generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) through doctrinal, comparative, and normative analysis of the European Union (EU), the United Kingdom (UK), and the United States (US). It covers copyright and related IP challenges in data acquisition, model training, output creation, and commercial deployment, as well as the distribution of control, transparency, attribution, and liability in each jurisdiction. The analysis reveals that the EU has several text-and-data-mining exceptions and copyright-policy and training-content-summary obligations for general-purpose AI providers, while the UK has a very limited non-commercial research exception and a unique statutory exception for computer-generated works, and the US is driven primarily by the human-authorship doctrine and fact-specific fair-use analysis. While these strategies offer valuable protections, none alone establish a comprehensive system of organisational control. The study thus suggests an auditing framework linked to the legal basis, data provenance, licenses, human contribution to creativity, output testing, documentation, accountability and escalation, and periodic reassessment, according to the proportionate degree of risk. Rather than harmonizing the three legal systems, the framework sets out a common organizational process for identifying and managing differences in the three legal systems to safeguard the rights holders and to allow for responsible innovation.

Background: Clinical teaching integrates theoretical knowledge with direct patient contact. However, in resource-limited settings, adequate patient contact is often compromised by inadequate clinical facilities, perennial industrial actions by healthcare workers, and limited access to rare or under-referred cases. The aim of this study was to develop an AI-generated visual clinic (a curated catalogue of videos) depicting motor rehabilitation in patients with stroke to help supplement real-world clinical teaching. Methods: An AI platform, Topmediai (https://www.topmediai.com/app/text-to-video/) was used to generate videos on constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT), motor imagery, sit-to-stand, over-ground gait training and treadmill gait training. The videos were edited and combined into an AI-generated visual clinic using CapCut (https://www.capcut.com/). Students and teachers were asked to rate the AI-generated visual clinic for: 1) Anatomical plausibility, 2) Procedural fidelity, 3) Rehabilitation accuracy, 4) Pedagogical clarity, and 5) Risk of learner misconception on a-5-point Likert scale, where, 1=low, 2= fair, 3=moderate, 4=high, and 5=very high. Results: A complete visual clinic demonstrating CIMT, motor imagery, sit-to-stand, over-ground gait training and treadmill gait training was produced. In addition, majority of the participants (both teachers and students), rated anatomical plausibility, procedural fidelity, rehabilitation accuracy and pedagogical clarity of the AI-generated visual clinic as high or very high; and risk of learner misconception as low or fair. Conclusion: It seems possible to generate clinically relevant videos of disease management using current AI text-to-video tools that can be catalogued into a “visual clinic” and used to support traditional clinical teaching.

documents.abstract: Abstract Acute otitis media (AOM) represents a prevalent infection in children globally, leading to considerable morbidity and imposing a substantial burden on healthcare systems. Prompt and precise diagnosis is critical to reducing complications, such as tympanic membrane perforation, hearing impairment, and excessive antibiotic prescribing. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, have created opportunities to enhance diagnostic accuracy and broaden access to care, especially in low-resource settings. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of AI-based systems for detecting AOM compared with conventional clinical diagnosis and to analyze their accuracy relative to human clinicians across different model architectures and diagnostic methods. Following PRISMA-DTA standards and PROSPERO registration, systematic searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore up to July 30, 2025. Eligible studies included human participants with suspected AOM, employed AI-driven diagnostic approaches, and used a clinical reference standard. The Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 tool assessed bias, and pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated using a bivariate random-effects model. Nine studies published between 2020 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. The pooled sensitivity and specificity were 91% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 77%–97%) and 99% (95% CI: 94%–100%), respectively. AI models overall matched or outperformed general practitioners and pediatricians, approaching otolaryngologist-level accuracy. AI-based tools have the potential to improve AOM detection, mitigate inequalities in healthcare access, and promote more effective diagnosis, particularly in underserved regions.

documents.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems for Arabic are evaluated almost exclusively with Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) queries, although users write in dialect. We study this mismatch with a parallel benchmark of 200 questions written in both MSA and Moroccan Darija over 3,054 Arabic Wikipedia passages. Dialectal queries lower hybrid-retrieval Recall@1 from 0.755 to 0.620, and the loss reaches the answers: with five retrieved passages, answer correctness falls from 0.810 to 0.690, mostly through additional refusals; part of this loss persists even when the gold passage is supplied directly, so retrieval is the larger but not the only component. Rewriting Darija queries into MSA does not help. Zero-shot cross-encoder reranking raises dialectal Recall@1 to 0.800 (MSA: 0.755 unreranked, 0.875 reranked) and lets a single retrieved passage replace five unreranked passages with no loss larger than five percentage points and a 3.7-fold shorter prompt. Because dialectal queries are retrieved with lower confidence, gating the reranker on the retriever’s score margin concentrates its cost on them without any dialect detection, retaining 94% of the benefit while reranking about half of the queries. The findings hold under a human-validated LLM judge (Cohen’s κ=0.797), Holm correction and three prompt wordings, and replicate judge-free on a second, Darija-trained generator. We release the benchmark, corpus, code and all result files.

Objective This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesize the results of randomized controlled trials to determine whether medication management approaches based on digital technologies and artificial intelligence/machine learning can indeed bring measurable clinical improvements in older adults with at least one chronic diseases. Methods To identify relevant RCTs, we performed a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, and other databases from their inception through June 30, 2026, for studies of digital and AI/ML-based medication management in older adults with at least one chronic diseases. All stages of study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers, applying the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool. Meta-analytic pooling was conducted via RevMan 5.4. Results Nineteen RCTs met the inclusion criteria, of which 6 were included in the meta-analysis and 13 in the descriptive synthesis. For medication adherence, three studies reported highly heterogeneous results ( I 2 = 97%), and because of this heterogeneity and the small number of studies, the data were not pooled; the individual study estimates ranged from SMD = −0.28–SMD = 1.89. For PIMs, only one study reported a comparable outcome; no pooled estimate was calculated. For hospitalization and mortality, the two included studies used different effect measures (HR and OR) and were therefore presented separately: Blum et al. reported an HR of 0.95 (95% CI 0.77–1.17), and Rieckert et al. reported an OR of 0.88 (95% CI 0.73–1.07). Conclusion The current body of evidence does not establish clinically meaningful benefits of digital or AI/ML-based medication management on hard endpoints such as hospitalization and mortality among older adults with at least one chronic diseases. For medication adherence, the evidence remains inconclusive and highly heterogeneous, and no reliable pooled estimate could be obtained. Given the pronounced heterogeneity and the limited pool of high-quality RCTs, current evidence is insufficient to establish clinical benefit for the routine implementation of digital or AI/ML-based medication management systems in geriatric care and further rigorously designed studies are warranted. Systematic review registration CRD420261460445.

The Internet and artificial intelligence (AI) have become deeply embedded in contemporary education, research and professional life. Their capacity to enhance learning efficiency and reduce access costs is undeniable. Yet these technologies have also generated significant negative externalities: students are increasingly distanced from printed textbooks and library-based study, turning instead to instantly available digital resources and generative AI tools. This shift has contributed to the erosion of deep reading, critical thinking and creativity. Drawing on recent empirical evidence, this article analyses the mechanisms through which screen-based reading and AI dependence undermine cognitive development, and argues that educational institutions must intervene through formal rules and regulations to minimise these externalities. It proposes a policy framework centred on the principle of preserving cognitive friction, encompassing curriculum design, pedagogical norms and assessment reform.

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how Industry 4.0 technologies reshape servitization and service-oriented manufacturing within digitally transforming supply chains. While digital servitization is often associated with technologies such as IoT, artificial intelligence, cloud platforms, analytics, and digital twins, the chapter argues that technology adoption alone is insufficient to generate service-oriented performance. Drawing on service-dominant logic, business model innovation, supply chain integration, socio-technical systems thinking, and dynamic capabilities theory, the chapter develops a theory-informed model explaining how manufacturers sense digital service opportunities, seize them through Industry 4.0-enabled service offerings, and reconfigure supply chain relationships around lifecycle value creation. The model is applied to an anonymous industrial equipment manufacturing case that illustrates the transition from product sales and reactive maintenance toward predictive maintenance, remote diagnostics, lifecycle service agreements, and recurring service revenue. The chapter contributes by positioning digital servitization as a capability-driven supply chain transformation and highlights practical conditions related to data governance, supplier readiness, customer trust, cybersecurity, and service-oriented performance measurement.

This study investigates the realisation and interactional functions of directive speech acts in researcher–AI communication through a reflexive case study of an academic journal submission. While directive speech acts have been extensively examined in human–human institutional interactions, limited empirical attention has been paid to how directives are constructed and deployed when the addressee is an artificial intelligence (AI) system operating within digitally mediated academic workflows. As AI systems increasingly assist scholars in writing and navigating editorial platforms, it is necessary to examine how action, authority, and epistemic responsibility are negotiated in human–AI interactions. This study addresses this gap by analysing a naturally occurring dialogue between a researcher and ChatGPT during the real-time submission of a manuscript to an international Q1 journal. The dataset comprised a complete 46-turn interaction sequence, from which 16 researcher-initiated directive moves were identified as primary units of analysis. Adopting a qualitative reflexive case study design, the analysis draws on speech act theory (Searle, 1976), interactional epistemics (Heritage, 2012), and relational work (Locher & Watts, 2008) to examine the linguistic realisation and functional deployment of directives across submission stages. The findings reveal that directives are predominantly realised through interrogative constructions rather than bald imperatives. WH-questions (e.g., “What should I do?”) and yes/no interrogatives pragmatically function as action-eliciting moves, particularly at moments of procedural uncertainty. These interrogatives enable the researcher to seek guidance while mitigating imposition, constructing AI as a procedural authority without an overt command. In addition to interrogatives, mitigated imperatives (e.g. “please explain”) and declarative problem reports (e.g., “I clicked OK, but there is no response”) operate as directive resources, demonstrating that directive force is interactionally achieved rather than strictly encoded in the grammatical mood. Functionally, four directive categories emerged: procedural guidance, explanatory mediation, confirmation for epistemic risk management, and evaluative positioning. Procedural guidance directives are clustered during technically opaque stages, such as PDF generation and final approval. Explanatory directives seek clarification of institutional prompts, positioning AI as an interpretive mediator. Confirmation directives appear before irreversible actions, reflecting heightened epistemic caution. A smaller subset of evaluative directives solicits normative stances regarding open-access decisions, extending human–AI interaction into moral reasoning. Directive density increases in phases characterised by institutional opacity, suggesting a correlation between procedural risks and directive production. Notably, directives are consistently mitigated through relational address terms and politeness markers despite the AI’s nonhuman status. This persistence of mitigation indicates that relational framing may function as a routinised communicative schema rather than solely as a face-protecting adjustment. Overall, this study argues that directives in researcher–AI interactions operate as mechanisms of institutional navigation and epistemic regulation rather than coercive command structures, contributing to empirical insights into the emerging field of human–AI pragmatics.
