documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping academic work, yet its occupational health implications for academicians remain under-examined. The Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework offers a dual lens for understanding AI as both a performance-enhancing resource and a source of job demands, but no systematic review has applied this framework across the full spectrum of academic roles. Objective This systematic review examines how AI impacts academicians’ performance across four core domains—teaching, research, community engagement, and professional development—using the JD-R framework to understand AI's dual nature as both a resource and a demand. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines and the five-stage framework of Khan et al., 1 we systematically searched Scopus and Web of Science databases for empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. After screening 868 records, 30 peer-reviewed journal articles met the inclusion criteria. A two-phase coding approach (deductive and inductive) was employed, with intercoder reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.91) indicating strong agreement. Thematic analysis was guided by the JD-R framework. Results Teaching performance dominates the literature (70%), reflecting AI's immediate impact on instructional practices. AI functions as a job resource through enhanced personalized learning, assessment automation, and administrative efficiency when supported by self-efficacy, AI literacy, and institutional resources. However, AI creates significant job demands including academic integrity management, assessment redesign, continuous upskilling, and ethical dilemmas. Professional development (27%) exhibits the most severe demand-resource imbalance, with faculty experiencing skill obsolescence anxiety, technostress, and imposter syndrome. Research performance (20%) shows a relatively balanced profile, while community engagement (7%) remains critically understudied. Identity-threatening demands—academic integrity in teaching, authorship ambiguity in research, and skill obsolescence in professional development—generate disproportionate psychological strain requiring specialized buffers. Conclusions AI's impact on academic work is inherently dualistic, with outcomes determined by the balance between available resources and demand intensity. Psychological resources, particularly self-efficacy, emerge as the most powerful enablers mediating the effectiveness of institutional and knowledge resources. The review extends JD-R theory by identifying identity-threatening demands as a distinct demand category and proposing a Resource Cascade Model wherein distal organizational resources foster proximal psychological resources. Institutions must adopt systemic, autonomy-supportive interventions addressing the full spectrum of AI's impact on academic work.

The article substantiates the structure, assessment criteria and levels of managerial competence of preschool leaders in dual in-service training. Effective leadership practices in early childhood education, personal leadership resources and theories of workplace learning were comparatively analysed. Competence was interpreted as a two-dimensional construct formed at the intersection of four practice domains and four personal resources, and criteria and indicators were defined for each domain. A four-level scale based on the Dreyfus model and a development cycle linking the training institution with the preschool organisation were proposed.

Issue No. 69 of Rhetoric and Communications continues the tradition of publishing research findings obtained through both traditional and contemporary methods, focusing on new and rapidly evolving fields of analysis, such as artificial intelligence, digitalization, the media ecosystem, and changes in education at the university and school levels. This issue brings together 12 scholarly articles in two sections. The first one is titled “Communication in Media and Society”, and two of the articles in this section are devoted to fact-checking, a topical issue in contemporary media and communication studies. In one article, researchers Milen Filipov and Nilufar Sulaimonova present findings related to an analysis of fact-checking activities in the media in Kazakhstan. In the second article, Tihomira Doncheva presents the results of a study on fact-checking and the use of artificial intelligence. The second area of research focuses on the media in Bulgaria. Aneta Milkova examines the legal framework, the limits of media regulation, and communication. Tanya Dimova discusses the functions of the Bulgarian National Radio, emphasizing the cultural role of the “Hristo Botev” program while taking into account changes in the digital media landscape. Alexander Blagoev presents the results of a study on social identity in communication through memes and participation in online challenges. Damyan Bumbalov clarifies, from a theoretical and methodological perspective, the scope and content of the concept of “monumental sculpture” and its communicative functions in public space. The second section includes interesting publications in which rhetoric and communication are studied in university and school settings. Faculty members from two universities in Ukraine – Mykola Chursin, Halyna Shevchenko, Tetiana Antonenko, and Tetiana Zinovieva – present the results of a timely and in-depth theoretical review related to changes in higher education resulting from technological transformations and the rapid integration of artificial intelligence into the educational process. The topic of artificial intelligence is also addressed in several other articles. Radeya Gesheva analyzes the transformations in the didactics of foreign-language literature in the era of artificial intelligence, focusing on Italian literature, for the teaching of which she provides many excellent practical examples in terms of methodology. Rhetoric is explored in new and interesting fields from a scholarly and methodological perspective: art, theater, education, and teaching in academic and school settings. Evgenia Roeva presents the findings of a study on the application of rhetoric and public speaking in education and its intersections with educational theater when working with elementary school students. Ralitsa Bezhan presents the results of a study on fundamental rhetorical canons from Aristotle to the era of artificial intelligence, contemporary theatrical performances and productions, and chatbots. Irena Shunina presents, in a captivating and compelling manner, the rhetoric of the heart and ethics in Shalva Amonashvili’s humanistic pedagogy. Boyan Zahariev highlights the specifics of pedagogical communication when using the LEGO® Serious Play® method: spatial projections and social identity as the result of field observation and a pedagogical experiment with Roma students from a neighborhood school

Intelligent Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) has a pivotal place in sarcasm detection, given that sarcastic utterances may have an intended meaning that is not in the literal meaning of the spoken words. Sarcasm is also difficult to spot correctly since it varies not only in text but also in voice and other visual indicators like facial expression and body language. Unimodal sarcasm detection methods are generally limited by contextual ambiguity, the insensitivity of contextual paralinguistic cues, and decreased performance in situations where one modality is noisy or incomplete. These problems may cause unpredictable results and inadequate functionality in the real conversational context. To overcome these shortcomings, for sarcasm detection, we suggest an approach with different modalities which uses multi-modal cues like audio, video as well as text to provide complementary information from various communication channels. In the case of textual representation, the RoBERTa architecture was used to elicit deep contextual and semantic features of dialog transcripts. The HuBERT architecture was used to model acoustic features and is effective at representing speech representations in terms of prosodic and tonal variation based on sarcastic speech. Simultaneously, the ViViT architecture was used to process visual data and identify both spatial and temporal patterns of facial expressions and gestures in videos. Modality-specific feature representations are then combined with a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) based fusion strategy which decides best-found modality weights by minimizing classification loss. The fused representation is then optimized and then through the two-layer fully connected classifier to classify sarcasm. The suggested framework was evaluated with the publicly available MUStARD dataset. The model displayed an accuracy of 94% and the recall, precision and weighted F1-score were all equal to 0.94. Comparative evaluation also compared the proposed PSO-Multimodal Fusion Model with the unimodal models and also with the traditional multimodal fusion models such as attention-based model, Graph-based model, Generative Approach, LLM/Modeling-based model, and contrastive learning approach, and showed that the proposed multimodal fusion framework yields the highest weighted F1-score among the evaluated approaches. Experimental outcomes prove that the multimodal fusion methodology based on optimization enhances the performance of sarcasm detection in contrast to the unimodal and traditional fusion techniques, which indicate its efficiency in practical use in conversational AI.

Single-Pilot Operations (SPO) in commercial aviation raise critical safety challenges in complex, time-pressured situations where human expertise is paramount. This study investigates how AI-based Human-Autonomy Teaming (HAT) can support pilot decision-making under high workload, compromised situational awareness, and time pressure. In a high-fidelity Airbus A320 simulator, 22 airline pilots performed a fuel- and time-constrained approach scenario designed to challenge HAT’s operational effectiveness under four conditions: no assistance, on-demand AI, proactive AI, and proactive explainable AI. Workload (NASA-TLX) remained high across conditions, yet decision-making differed markedly. Without assistance, only 20% chose the safest landing option; with on-demand AI, 40%; and with proactive AI (both versions), 100%. Explainable AI yielded the highest scenario comprehension (75%), matching two-crew baseline performance. Proactive systems increased decision and SA related interactions, fostering a collaborative dynamic akin to traditional crew resource management. Thus, the results demonstrate that, in the context of SPO, proactive and explainable AI was associated with crew-level decision performance within the experimental scenario without adding cognitive load. Beyond the aeronautical domain, our results are of interest for the design of cognitive support systems for high-risk domains where teams composed of humans and AI must adapt in real time.

Teachers' limited competence in utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based digital media has hindered the effective implementation of innovative teaching practices and environmental projects. This community service program aimed to enhance teachers' knowledge and skills in developing AI-based instructional media. The program was conducted at State Senior High School 1 Koto Kampar Hulu and involved 29 teachers through educational seminars, workshops, hands-on practice, and mentoring using Canva AI, Gemini AI, and NotebookLM. Program effectiveness was evaluated using pretest-posttest assessments, N-Gain analysis, instructional media product evaluation, and participant satisfaction questionnaires. The results showed that the participants' mean score increased from 47.0 to 78.9, with an N-Gain score of 0.6, indicating a moderate level of improvement. All participants (100%) demonstrated increased knowledge following the training. Furthermore, every participant successfully developed at least one AI-based instructional medium, such as a poster or infographic, that was ready for implementation in classroom instruction and environmental projects. These findings indicate that the training effectively enhanced teachers' digital competencies and their ability to integrate AI technologies into teaching and learning practices

documents.abstract: Technical, social, avant-garde, global, and cognitive pressures are driving the adoption of new technologies characterized by constant updates and automation most notably generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents. While the stated intention is to augment and enhance human capabilities regarding complex challenges, skills, and critical thinking rather than replacing them recent empirical evidence suggests the actual trend is moving in the opposite direction, to the detriment of consumers. This study analyzes the flaws and risks stemming from the use and misuse of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose intervention frameworks before they become irreversibly entrenched in a fragile structure within the technology adoption cycle. It explores phenomena such as the atrophy of technical skills, the productivity paradox, cognitive offloading, over-reliance on automated systems, and the irony of automation, drawing on evidence from randomized controlled trials and large-scale surveys conducted between 2025 and 2026. This analysis examines the critical failures and systemic risks of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose regulatory and operational intervention frameworks before their negative effects become irreversibly embedded in the labor market and social fabric. Identifying these risk vectors early allows for the design of guidelines that restore human control, ensuring technology acts as a genuine complement rather than an agent of cognitive and professional erosion. Furthermore, there is high demand for courses, diploma programs, and workshops focused on critical thinking, reflecting a growing awareness of the need to pursue them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: On 25 May 2026, Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas became the first papal encyclical on artificial intelligence, declaring that lethal decisions cannot be entrusted to artificial systems and calling for a shared international framework to govern military AI. It states these principles but does not operationalise them. This article develops that operational framework. Applying Catholic social doctrine (human dignity and agency, subsidiarity, prudence, intentionality, the common good, and the protection of noncombatants) to military AI, it translates the encyclical's commitments into concrete requirements for autonomous weapons, targeting systems, and alliance interoperability. It grounds the argument in the nuclear precedent, where Catholic ethics shaped doctrine as it formed, and more briefly in chemical and biological weapons prohibition. Engaging just war theory, NATO's Principles of Responsible Use, recent military wargaming, and a leading AI provider's treatment of a catastrophic strike as consistent with its self-declared “red lines,” it shows where Catholic ethics is more demanding than procedural compliance. It then proposes institutional mechanisms: a tiered deliberation framework, proportionality dossiers, ethics review boards, and NATO-level coordination. Building ethical architecture before deployment, the article argues, serves strategic as well as moral interests.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
