documents.abstract: Human rights have become a pervasive vocabulary in Indian legal and social science research, yet the structure and direction of this expanding literature have rarely been examined systematically. This review maps 457 Scopus-indexed journal articles on human rights with at least one Indian institutional affiliation, published between 2016 and 2026, using performance analysis and science-mapping techniques. Annual output grew more than five-fold, from 14 articles in 2016 to 75 in 2025 and 82 in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of about 20.5 per cent. The literature is highly dispersed: the 457 articles appeared in 318 journals, 36 of which account for one-third of the output, and 93 per cent of the 1,516 authors contributed only one article. Citation impact is modest (median one citation; 36.3 per cent uncited; dataset h-index 22). Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies six principal clusters: constitutional equality and discrimination; public health, pandemic and surveillance; artificial intelligence and intellectual property; climate change, displacement and the rights of nature; data protection and international law; and sustainable development and consumer protection. Thematic evolution shows a shift from trade-related intellectual property and health policy in 2016-2020 to COVID-19 and constitutional dignity in 2021-2023, and to artificial intelligence, data protection and climate change in 2024-2026. In contrast, the institutions through which rights are enforced receive very little attention: police, prisons and custody appear in about 2 per cent of articles, caste and Dalit concerns in 2.2 per cent, and the National Human Rights Commission in only three articles (0.7 per cent), none of which takes a commission as its object of study. The review argues that Indian human rights scholarship has undergone a “technological and regulatory turn” that risks neglecting the accountability of the coercive state, and proposes a research agenda centred on enforcement institutions, caste and gender intersections, and data-driven evaluation.

The introduction of innovative products is a critical driver of competitive advantage in highly turbulent technological environments. The objective of this article is to systematically analyze the recent literature on the marketing strategies that optimize the acceptance and performance of such innovations. Using a systematic-narrative methodology, a final corpus of 20 scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025 in high-impact databases such as Scopus and Web of Science was selected. The results reveal that commercial success does not reside exclusively in technical superiority, but in the creative configuration of an integrated marketing mix, where packaging design, dynamic pricing, and the diversification of channels toward e-commerce reduce adoption barriers. A strategic shift is identified, moving from traditional launch models toward agile, iterative, and niche approaches that prioritize user co-creation to mitigate perceived risk. Furthermore, functional communication and educational pre-announcements emerge as essential cognitive mechanisms for reducing consumer resistance to change in the face of radical innovations. It is concluded that dynamic organizational capabilities, enhanced by Marketing 4.0 and artificial intelligence, are crucial for personalizing the value proposition and ensuring product sustainability in global markets.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to transform clinical practice, but its adoption coincides with a longstanding decline in bedside medicine. Herein, we argue that reintroducing Oslerian principles into medical training may be essential to ensure that technological progress does not come at the expense of the physician-patient relationship. Throughout, we use the term AI to refer to tools built on algorithms, from risk calculators and predictive models to large language models, that produce predictions, classifications or recommendations. These tools have no agency of their own: they operate only on the data supplied to them, and their implementation depends on how clinicians and institutions design and deploy them.William Osler never saw an algorithm. He died in 1919, a century before "artificial intelligence" entered the clinical vocabulary. And yet no figure in the history of medicine is better equipped to tell us what we are about to lose 1 . Osler's central achievement was a discipline of the mind: the conviction that the practice of medicine must rest on direct observation of the patient and on the relationship between patient and physician. We argue that this discipline is now under direct threat, and that AI tools, as currently deployed, tend to hasten its erosion rather than reverse it -unless we act deliberately to stop it. In fact, the physician-patient relationship has already been reshaped by decades of patient access to medical information through the internet and social media. This shift has been amplified by the development of health-related AI tools, which increase patients' knowledge but also expose them to misinformation and misinterpretation. Nowadays, patients often arrive at the clinical encounter having already formed their own interpretations about their disease, which directly impacts the dialogue with the physician from the very first minutes of the encounter -a dynamic Osler never had to confront. Oslerian principles must therefore be adapted to this new reality, in which both physician and patient increasingly approach the clinical encounter already shaped by algorithms.Clarifying what AI can do -and will not do in the foreseeable future AI tools can go extraordinarily far in the medical process -synthesizing literature at a scale no human can match, flagging patterns in imaging and pathology that trained eyes miss, drafting notes, triaging risk, generating differential diagnoses, and suggesting therapeutic options in seconds. None of this is in serious dispute anymore, and clinicians who dismiss it outright are being unrealistic.On the other hand, it is illusory to imagine that AI will, in the foreseeable future, replace clinical observation and the personal relationship between doctor and patient. This needs to be said plainly, not hedged. Diagnosis by patternmatching on data is not the same as sitting at the bedside of anxious patients, watching how they behave, picking up on what they leave unsaid, and actually building the trust that makes adherence possible. Whatever level of performance AI models will achieve in the future, they will remain trained on the past, and no model can substitute for what happens, uniquely, in the present, between two people.There is also a more technical reason why bedside medicine remains indispensable: AI can only reason about the reality that has been captured and digitized. An algorithm implicitly assumes that what is absent from the record does not exist. Because important information reaches the record only if a physician observes it, an algorithm working from an incomplete record can return a seemingly precise but inaccurate output, creating an illusion of certainty. Oslerian observation is therefore not a nostalgic complement to AI but a technical prerequisite for its validity: no AI tool can compensate for a hurried or incomplete examination. Far from making clinical skills obsolete, AI demands sharper skills in listening, observation and physical examination.Losing the lessons learned at the bedside is not a hypothetical risk, nor is it a new one. For decades, medical departments have been organized around organ systems and specialized technologies. This process of specialization and subspecialization -a transformation that long predates the current wave of AI adoption -has produced remarkable diagnostic and therapeutic advances, but it has also fragmented the physician's view of the patient as a whole and made a holistic approach harder to sustain. Another powerful driver of this change has been the growth of administrative and documentation burden: in ambulatory practice, a time-and-motion study found that physicians spend nearly two hours on electronic health records and desk work for every hour of direct clinical face time with patients 2 , and administrative burden has been associated with lower intrinsic motivation among physicians and poorer patient-reported experience of care 3 .Consistent with this, studies among internal medicine trainees have documented a clear decline in direct time with patients for well over a decade 4 , and the trend is still underway today in several disciplines. For example, in hematologic malignancies, where AI-based tools are being rapidly adopted to guide diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions 5 , physicians increasingly spend more time in offices in front of computer screens -reviewing algorithmic outputs, multiomic profiles, and risk calculators -often making therapeutic decisions before they examine the patient, so that the consultation risks becoming a confirmation of a decision already made elsewhere, rather than the encounter from which the decision should emerge. Deployed carelessly, AI tools are likely to deepen this pattern rather than correct it. Many current incentives push in that direction: institutions will reward the efficiency of deciding early, physicians will gravitate toward the workflow that is faster and less cognitively taxing, and the tools themselves are easiest to deploy on data that are already structured and available before the visit. Left to market and workflow pressures alone, AI is unlikely to restore the clinical encounter and may further hollow it out. This is the central danger. However, AI can also work in the opposite direction. In a recent randomized trial, ambient AI scribes, which transcribe the consultation and draft the clinical note, were associated with reduced physician burnout, and doctors reported that the technology allowed them to engage better with their patients 6 . Such tools can return the physician's attention from the screen to the patientprovided that the time they free is deliberately protected for the clinical encounter.This is precisely why Osler's teaching should not be treated as an outdated precept, but as the specific countermeasure this moment requires. We argue that it should be urgently reintroduced as a structural component of clinical education, integrated into, not appended to, the technical curriculum. Three Oslerian principles should anchor that effort: "Listen to the patient; he is telling you the diagnosis." What the physician personally learns at the patient's bedside should always come first -a principle physicians in subspecialty training are especially at risk of losing, as AI output can easily become the main input they consult before reaching a conclusion. AI output should inform that conclusion but not replace it."Medicine is learned by the bedside and not in the classroom." Osler's most consequential reform was moving medical education out of the lecture hall and to the patient's side. A century later, the direction of travel has reversed: trainees now often learn to interpret data before they learn to examine a patient. That sequence needs to be corrected, with protected, unhurried bedside time built into training and explicitly shielded from the pressure to consult the algorithm first. "Imperturbability." In his famous 1889 address, Aequanimitas 7 , Osler used this word to describe the calm and steady judgment a physician needs when facing suffering, urgency and clinical uncertainty. Applied to the output of AI, the same discipline must hold: neither adopting it blindly, a failure known as automation bias 8 , nor dismissing it out of hand, but checking it as rigorously as any other clinical evidence, including against what the physician has personally observed.These principles cannot be reintroduced as a simple return to an earlier era; they must be adapted to a clinical environment now shaped not only by AI but also by electronic health records, an ever-expanding volume of diagnostic data, and patients arriving informed -and sometimes misinformed. The task for training programs is not to teach learners to resist these developments but to integrate them without displacing direct observation and reasoning. Concretely, this could include bedside practice that requires trainees to form their own clinical impression before consulting AI output, case studies comparing bedside findings with AI-generated information, exercises showing how omissions in the history or examination alter an algorithm's output, and communication exercises on discussing AI- derived information with patients. These skills should be embedded into formal assessment and not treated as incidental.Discussions on "AI and the future of medicine" too often lead to wishful thinking that is very unlikely to be implemented. Instead, they should lead to concrete proposals, such as treating the clinical encounter as a parameter to be measured in academic medical centers. Time at the bedside is a necessary but insufficient indicator, since more time does not automatically translate into better care. We therefore propose mixed metrics combining the time physicians actually spend with patients, the diagnostic accuracy of the physician working with AI compared with either alone, and patients' perceptions of empathy and trust assessed with validated instruments such as the Consultation and Relational Empathy (CARE) measure 9 .William Osler would have welcomed the advent of AI in medicine, but he would have insisted that every AI tool be held to a single non-negotiable question: does it bring the physician closer to the patient, or does it interpose itself between them? On present evidence, in disciplines already reorganized around screens and algorithms, many AI deployments are failing that test 10 . The remedy is not to slow the technology down. It is to speed up, urgently, the reintroduction of Osler's principles into the training of every physician who will use it.

Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The aim of the article is to reconstruct the lay conceptions held by students of early childhood and pre-primary education regarding generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and its potential role in education. The study is grounded in the constructivist-interpretive paradigm, adopting an understanding of learning as a process of active construction and negotiation of meanings. The empirical material was collected using a questionnaire consisting of open, exploratory questions. The participants were students who had already completed coursework related to didactics but had not yet taken courses on modern technologies. A non-probability purposive sampling strategy was applied. The collected data were analyzed using interpretative thematic analysis. The results reveal tension in students’ common understandings of GenAI. On the one hand, GenAI is perceived as a tool that increases teacher effectiveness and facilitates access to information. On the other hand, the same feature raises concerns about limiting students’ cognitive independence. The results further suggest that future teachers’ ways of thinking about GenAI may be closely related to their understanding of the nature of learning and educational culture. Therefore, the study highlights the need to incorporate reflection on GenAI into teacher education – not as a technical issue, but as a didactic one.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction: Physiotherapy education in India is transitioning to a competency-based curriculum that emphasises selfdirected learning. Academic motivation is a key learner-related factor that influences academic outcomes. However, evidence on motivational profiles across academic performance groups remains limited, especially among physiotherapy students. Understanding these differences may facilitate targeted educational support to improve academic outcomes. Aim: To assess academic motivation and compare advanced, average, and Slow Performers (SLP) among undergraduate physiotherapy students. Materials and Methods: The present multicentre crosssectional study was conducted from March 2025 to December 2025 in private physiotherapy colleges affiliated with Maharashtra University of Health Sciences located in Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. A complete enumerative sampling technique was used to recruit 509 eligible first-year physiotherapy undergraduates. Students who took the first formative exam were included. Based on exam scores, students were classified as advanced (top 20%), average (middle 60%), or SLPs (bottom 20%). Data were collected using the Academic Motivation Scale via Google Forms and Analysed applying the Mann-Whitney U test and Kruskal-Wallis H test with Bonferroni correction (p<0.017). A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results: A total of 450 participants were included for the final analysis, comprising 74 males (16.44%) and 376 females (83.56%). Significant differences were observed among the three academic performance groups for intrinsic motivation to know (H=13.25, p=0.001) and amotivation (H=13.97, p=0.001). Post-hoc analysis showed significant differences in intrinsic motivation to know between advanced and SLPs, and between average and SLPs, while amotivation differed significantly between advanced and SLPs. Conclusion: The findings of the present study demonstrate that advanced performers exhibited higher intrinsic and lower amotivation than SLPs, although the differences were small. Moreover, extrinsic motivation types did not differ. Integrating early assessment of academic motivation and autonomysupportive learning environments may help reduce amotivation and enhance learner engagement.

This qualitative study examined how secondary school English teachers in Philippine public schools negotiate and reconstruct pedagogy in response to artificial intelligence (AI). Using Constructivist Grounded Theory, the study drew on intensive semi-structured interviews with seven English teachers from selected public secondary schools under the Schools Division Office of Batangas City. Initial and focused coding, constant comparison, memo writing, and theoretical integration generated seven interrelated categories: continually recalibrating pedagogical practice; protecting the learning work from technological substitution; reconstructing assessment to make learning and authorship visible; negotiating ethical boundaries through contextual professional judgment; building adaptive capacity through collegial and institutional support; cultivating critical AI literacy while preserving human voice and communication; and mediating AI access to preserve equity and inclusive participation. Findings indicate that responsible adaptation involves recursive, context-sensitive professional judgment. Teachers evaluated whether AI supported intended competencies, preserved valid assessment and authorship, maintained ethical safeguards, and enabled equitable participation. The categories informed the emergent AI-Responsive English Pedagogy Framework. The study concludes that responsible integration requires bounded technological augmentation, professional learning, flexible institutional guidance, assessment redesign, and protection of authentic language learning.

G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) modulate diverse hormonal, metabolic, neural, and immunological signaling processes. Their age-dependent decline accounts for many fundamental hallmarks of aging, including low-grade inflammation (inflammaging), mitochondrial failure and energy dysregulation, genomic instability and epigenetic dysregulation, dysregulated cellular communication, loss of proteostasis, and cellular senescence. Consequently, GPCR dysfunction underpins nearly all chronic, age-related diseases, including cardiovascular disease, cancer, various endocrine disorders, and neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases. Therefore, the GPCR network (“GPCR-ome”) constitutes a central, druggable, “mega-trophic” regulator of human healthspan. Individual GPCRs present numerous therapeutic targets for specific conditions, many of which are already being exploited, while others show future promise. Alongside this disease-centric approach, the GPCR-ome offers the more radical opportunity to rebalance entire signaling networks to simultaneously correct the multisystem pathological effects of aging itself. Here, we outline a transformative paradigm for network-level, GPCR-based geroprotection that employs artificial intelligence, digital twins, and quantum computational methods to design biased agonists, allosteric or multitarget modulators, heteromer-selective ligands, and polypharmacological strategies to mitigate and manage age-related disorders. We also explore how combinatorial GPCR-based strategies (e.g., coupled with senolytic, metabolic, or regenerative medicines) hold compelling promise to delay multiple hallmarks of aging and enable personalized anti-aging GPCR therapies based on multiomic biomarkers.
topics: Genetics, Aging, and Longevity in Model Organisms

documents.abstract: Abstract The NOAA-NASA Joint Archive (NNJA pronounced like the word ninja) is a publicly accessible, curated collection of Earth system observations spanning 1979 to present, created to accelerate reanalysis production, support development of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, and enable access to the observational record underlying modern reanalyses. The archive encompasses atmospheric satellite radiances and conventional measurements, in-situ ocean profiles, sea ice concentrations and freeboard retrievals, and land surface observations from over 60 sensors provided by NOAA, NASA, and their partners. The number of atmospheric records increases from around 10 6 observations per day in 1979 to around 10 8 in the modern era. The dataset extends into near-real time through continuous archival of the NOAA operational data. NNJA observations are distributed through Amazon Web Services in formats compatible with established data assimilation systems and are accompanied by channel-level black and white lists that capture the quality history of the satellite record. Data integrity is verified through a three-tier process: file-level metadata checks, cross-validation against existing black and white lists from prior NOAA and NASA reanalyses, and a comparison of assimilation statistics with reference reanalysis and operational products. To lower barriers for the machine learning community, a companion dataset (NNJA-AI) transforms NNJA observations from legacy formats to column-oriented Apache Parquet, enabling sufficient large-scale queries and direct integration with AI training workflows. This article describes the creation, verification, and curation of the NNJA dataset, document its current scope and known limitations, and discusses its role as a shared observational infrastructure for the next generation of U.S. reanalyses.

Numerical analysis serves as the fundamental pillar of modern engineering modeling, providing the mathematical and computational tools necessary to transform complex physical equations into practical numerical solutions. This study reviews contemporary applications of numerical analysis in enhancing engineering models, focusing on methodological advancements in solving partial differential equations, data-driven model order reduction techniques, adaptive mesh methods, and machine learning-based surrogate models. The study employs a synthetic analytical approach that combines a review of recent literature with an analysis of empirical results from various numerical methods, addressing hybrid models that integrate traditional techniques with artificial intelligence. The analysis demonstrates that combining traditional numerical analysis methods with artificial intelligence and reduced-order models has revolutionized the ability of engineers to simulate complex multiphysics systems with unprecedented accuracy and computational efficiency; hybrid models have achieved computational speedups ranging from 72 to 522 times compare to traditional methods. Furthermore, the study addresses challenges related to computational cost and solution sensitivity to initial conditions, examining cutting-edge innovative solutions such as physicsinformed neural networks and causality-based learning. The study concludes that future trends in this field are shifting towards the development of hybrid models that combine analytical accuracy with computational speed, with an increasing emphasis on generalization capabilities beyond the training data. This opens up broad prospects for digital engineering and digital twin applications across the industrial, energy, and infrastructure sectors. The study offers a comprehensive perspective on the development of engineering models using advanced numerical analysis techniques and identifies promising future research directions in this vital field.
topics: Advanced Numerical Methods in Computational Mathematics

documents.abstract: This article examines the motivational, individual psychological, social, and organizational-pedagogical factors influencing the development of students' intellectual abilities through metacognitive strategies. A total of 280 students from the 7th and 9th grades participated in the study. The Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), developed by P.R. Pintrich, A.F. Smith, T. Garcia, and W.J. McKeachie, along with H. Gardner's Multiple Intelligences assessment method, was used to investigate correlations between motivational factors and different types of intelligence. The findings revealed positive correlations between intrinsic goal orientation, task value, self-efficacy for learning performance, elaboration, critical thinking, and metacognitive self-regulation and linguistic, logical-mathematical, and personal intelligences. Furthermore, the study highlights the significance of students' age-related characteristics, independent thinking, reflective abilities, and the educational environment in the application of metacognitive strategies. The findings substantiate the importance of psychological and pedagogical approaches aimed at strengthening intrinsic motivation, improving self-monitoring, and enhancing reflective activities to promote the development of students' intellectual potential.

documents.abstract: Abstract Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

documents.abstract: In talent pathways that formally include both sexes, it remains unclear whether boys and girls selected into the same pathway accumulate comparable football activity. This study aimed to (1) describe sex-stratified self-reported weekly football exposure and motivational regulation among 103 players (51 girls, 52 boys; 13.8 ± 0.9 years) selected for one regional division of a Norwegian national youth talent development program, and (2) describe age-cohort patterns across the ≤13-, 14- and 15-year cohorts. Players reported weekly football hours and sessions during the preparation period and competitive season. Because the dataset lacked club- and training-group identifiers, observations could not be assumed independent; the study is therefore descriptive and exploratory: sex-stratified exposure and motivational regulation are summarized as median [interquartile range, IQR], age-cohort exposure as mean ± SD, and between-sex patterns as differences in central tendency rather than as hypothesis tests. In this sample, boys reported higher total weekly football exposure than girls (median 10.8 vs. 7.0 h), with a proportionally larger difference for self-organized than organized activity. Boys reported slightly higher intrinsic motivation and identified regulation, whereas girls reported slightly higher amotivation, external regulation and introjected regulation; these differences were small relative to the scale range, and both groups reported high intrinsic motivation and low amotivation in absolute terms. Because players were drawn from shared but unmodeled development environments in a cross-sectional design, the findings are descriptive only: equal formal selection did not coincide with equal football exposure, particularly in self-organized activity, generating hypotheses for future cluster-aware studies.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly influencing sustainability education by providing dynamic tools that foster systems thinking, data literacy, ethical reasoning, and creative problem solving. Yet despite growing experimentation with AI in teaching and learning, there remains a notable gap in practice-based frameworks that guide educators in integrating AI into ESD in ethically grounded and pedagogically purposeful ways. Addressing this need, this chapter explores how AI can be thoughtfully integrated into Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) through innovative pedagogical approaches. Drawing on teaching cases and reflective analysis, it introduces the IDEA (Innovation, Design, Evaluation, and Anchoring) framework as a structured yet flexible guide for integrating AI into practice. The framework is illustrated through practice-informed vignettes, including the use of generative AI for futures thinking, machine learning for environmental data analysis, AI-powered feedback in ethics debates, and co-designed projects with pre-service teachers. These examples highlight both the affordances and tensions of using AI in higher education and teacher preparation programs. The IDEA framework encourages educators to critically examine how AI tools align with sustainability goals, support meaningful learning outcomes, and surface issues of ethics, equity, and digital competence. Situating AI not as a disruptive novelty but as a pedagogical mediator, the chapter contributes to the discourse on ESD and the responsible integration of emerging technologies. Drawing on interdisciplinary scholarship, it reflects on implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and education policy, offering actionable recommendations for creating ethical, inclusive, and future-facing learning environments.

This study was initiated by the uneven learning motivation among junior high school students in Coding and Artificial Intelligence (CAI) subjects. The research aims to enhance students’ learning motivation through a project-based gamification strategy. The method employed was Classroom Action Research (CAR) based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, conducted in two cycles with 31 students as subjects. The learning process implemented Project-Based Learning (PjBL) integrated with six gamification elements (clear goals, points, challenges, badges, feedback, and leaderboards) through a simple Scratch game development project. Data were collected using an adapted Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), observations, field notes, and documentation, and analyzed descriptively. The results showed an increase in students’ learning motivation, with the classical average rising from 3.06 (76.39%) in the pre-cycle to 3.24 (81.00%) in Cycle I and 3.38 (84.39%) in Cycle II, and all motivation aspects improving. Students reaching the minimum “High” criterion (score ≥ 3.00) increased from 51.61% (16 students) in the pre-cycle to 77.42% (24 students) in Cycle I, and reached the classical success target at 80.65% (25 students) in Cycle II. In Cycle II, a layered troubleshooting strategy using a Generative AI chatbot as a coding assistant, followed by peer feedback, appeared to support more persistent and independent problem-solving, although the gains were moderate and uneven across students, and self-regulation remained the lowest-scoring aspect (3.09). In conclusion, project-based gamification was accompanied by an increase in junior high school students’ learning motivation in CAI subjects.

Penelitian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh penerapan model pembelajarn Discovery Learning yang belum terlaksana secara optimal, serta penggunaan Artificial Intelligence dalam pembelajaran yang masih bersifat umum, belum terarah, dan belum dimanfaatkan secara inovatif sebagai pendukung proses belajar peserta didik. Kondisi tersebut menyebabkan peserta didik masih mengalami kesulitan dalam memahami konsep-konsep kimia yang bersifat abstrak. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui pengaruh penerapan model Discovery Learning berbantuan Artificial Intelligence terhadap hasil belajar peserta didik pada materi teori asam basa. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan metode pre-experimental design dan desain One Group Pretest-Posttest Design. Sampel penelitian terdiri atas 35 peserta didik kelas X.E di SMK SMAK Makassar yang dipilih menggunakan teknik purposive sampling. Teknik pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui tes hasil belajar berupa pretest dan posttest. Analisis data dilakukan menggunakan statistik deskriptif dan inferensial melalui uji prasyarat yakni uji normalitas, dilanjutkan uji hipotesis nonparametric yakni Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test, dan analisis N-gain. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa penerapan model Discovery Learning berbantuan Artificial Intelligence memberikan pengaruh terhadap peningkatan hasil belajar peserta didik. Nilai N-gain berada pada kategori tinggi sehingga model pembelajaran tersebut efektif dalam meningkatkan hasil belajar peserta didik pada materi teori asam basa.

Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis pengaruh strategi guru dalam pembelajaran deep learning dan penggunaan Artificial Intelligence (AI) terhadap hasil belajar siswa melalui self-regulated learning (SRL) sebagai variabel mediasi di SMA Negeri 2 Balikpapan. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan jenis penelitian eksplanatori. Data dikumpulkan melalui kuesioner, observasi, dan dokumentasi, kemudian dianalisis menggunakan metode Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) dengan bantuan perangkat lunak SmartPLS. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa pendekatan pembelajaran mendalam guru berpengaruh secara signifikan terhadap self-regulated learning dan hasil belajar siswa, namun tidak berpengaruh secara langsung terhadap hasil belajar siswa. Penggunaan AI juga terbukti berpengaruh signifikan terhadap self-regulated learning dan hasil belajar siswa. Selain itu, self-regulated learning berpengaruh secara signifikan terhadap hasil belajar. Hasil uji mediasi menunjukkan bahwa belajar yang dikontrol sendiri berfungsi sebagai mediator penuh pada hubungan antara guru strategi dan hasil belajar, serta berfungsi sebagai mediator parsial pada hubungan antara penggunaan AI dan hasil belajar. Oleh karena itu, dapat disimpulkan bahwa penguatan pembelajaran yang dikontrol sendiri merupakan komponen penting dalam penerapan strategi pembelajaran mendalam dan penggunaan AI untuk meningkatkan hasil belajar siswa

Enterprises increasingly rely on heterogeneous documents, relational databases, and analytical systems to support information retrieval and business decision-making. Integrating large language models (LLMs) with these sources introduces challenges in evidence reliability, analytical correctness, access control, and operational resilience. This paper presents PIU Smart Intelligence Agents, a security-aware multi-agent architecture designed to integrate enterprise document intelligence, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, document summarization, naturallanguage-to-SQL analytics, key performance indicator (KPI) generation, and conversational AI within a common application and governance framework. The proposed architecture organizes specialized AI capabilities around shared services for authentication, authorization, request validation, provider integration, observability, and controlled data access. Its document-processing workflow encompasses file validation, text extraction, optical character recognition for scanned documents, normalization, chunking, embedding generation, and vector-based indexing. The structured-analytics workflow separates schema-aware query generation from SQL validation, restricted database execution, and result interpretation. The architecture also addresses provider compatibility, timeout handling, failure recovery, document lifecycle management, and traceability of generated outputs. The source implementation reports 1,242 automated tests passed and two integration tests skipped. These results are reported implementation evidence and have not been independently reproduced. The available evidence does not establish comprehensive external RAG benchmark performance, quantitative correctness across all agents, independently validated security effectiveness, or production-scale performance and recovery guarantees. Accordingly, this study presents an integrated engineering architecture and identifies a reproducible evaluation framework for assessing its effectiveness. The principal contribution is the systematic integration of heterogeneous enterprise AI capabilities with explicit governance and validation requirements, rather than the introduction of a new learning or retrieval algorithm. Future work should prioritize agent-specific correctness testing, retrieval and answer-quality benchmarks, adversarial security evaluation, controlled load testing, and recovery verification.

Dental imaging is fundamental to diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up in Oral Medicine and Maxillofacial Radiology. Although conventional radiographic interpretation remains dependent on professional expertise, diagnostic performance may be influenced by observer variability, image quality, workload, and the subtle nature of early pathological changes. The development of Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), has introduced new approaches for automated analysis of dental and maxillofacial images. This narrative review discusses the evolution, principles, applications, clinical relevance, limitations, and future directions of deep learning in dental imaging, with emphasis on intraoral radiography, panoramic radiography, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), and related imaging modalities. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have demonstrated applications in dental caries detection, periodontal bone assessment, periapical lesion detection, tooth identification and numbering, jaw lesion analysis, anatomical segmentation, and treatment planning. More advanced architectures, including U-Net, residual networks, object-detection models, three-dimensional CNNs, and emerging transformer-based systems, have expanded the scope of automated image interpretation. However, the rapid growth of research has also highlighted important limitations, including small and heterogeneous datasets, inconsistent annotation, retrospective study designs, limited external validation, algorithmic bias, and difficulties in explaining model predictions. Importantly, high algorithmic accuracy does not necessarily translate into clinical effectiveness. Future research should therefore focus on diverse multicentre datasets, external and prospective validation, explainable AI, multimodal systems, ethical governance, and meaningful human-AI collaboration. Deep learning is most appropriately viewed as an adjunctive clinical decision-support technology that complements rather than replaces professional diagnostic judgment.

documents.abstract: This research aims to anticipate potential future transformations in the television production industry amidst rapid technological advancements and to examine their impact on production quality and the efficiency of technical and professional processes. It also seeks to identify the key challenges media organizations face in adopting and integrating modern technologies into television production environments. The study focuses on three main areas: the role of modern technologies in enhancing television production quality; the technical, human, economic, and organizational challenges associated with their adoption; and the impact of artificial intelligence applications—a prominent feature of contemporary technological transformation—on production process efficiency. The study employed a descriptive methodology, utilizing a questionnaire to gather data from a sample of 400 participants—professionals and staff within the radio and television sectors. The sample encompassed broadcasters, directors, editors, producers, engineers, technicians, media researchers, and marketing and advertising personnel, as well as channel and station managers and consultants in technology and IT. This approach enabled an examination of diverse professional perspectives regarding the current state of technological transformations and their potential future trends. The research findings indicate that modern technological advancements—particularly artificial intelligence applications—play a significant role in evolving television production processes. This is achieved by enhancing audio and visual quality, developing visual effects, improving content management efficiency, automating certain operational tasks, and minimizing human error. Conversely, the results reveal a number of challenges that could hinder the adoption of these technologies, most notably high costs and the need to upgrade the professional and technical skills of the workforce. In light of these findings, the research discusses potential future transformations in the television production industry—specifically the shift toward smarter, more flexible production environments, the reshaping of certain professional roles, and the increasing reliance on advanced technical solutions across various stages of production.

Acute stroke alerts are frequently activated for non-cerebrovascular conditions, creating false positives that strain resources and increase diagnostic uncertainty. We developed machine learning models integrating large-language models, structured electronic health record data, and clinical time-series features to predict acute intracranial vascular event (AIVE) at stroke alert activation. Using retrospective stroke alerts from the Mount Sinai Health System (2011–2021), we extracted demographics, comorbidities, medications, vital signs, laboratory results, and clinical notes documented before alert activation. AIVE was defined using radiographic gold standards as a composite of acute cerebrovascular and selected acute intracranial diagnoses. Notes were modeled using Clinical-Longformer, MxBAI embeddings with a feed-forward neural network, and BioWordVec embeddings with logistic regression; structured-data models used complementary hyperparameter-tuned workflows. Model outputs were combined in a late-fusion stacked ensemble and evaluated on internal and within-system held-out hospital test sets. Among 16,512 stroke alerts, 9,013 (55.6%) were due to AIVE. The multimodal model achieved an AUROC of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.71–0.75), positive predictive value of 0.68, sensitivity of 0.76, F1-score of 0.72, and specificity of 0.56 on internal testing, with similar held-out hospital performance. This approach may support post-activation stroke-alert risk stratification and reduce false-positive evaluations.

Introduction: Volatile operating environments create demand uncertainty, supplier disruptions, delivery delays, geopolitical shocks, and other events that can negatively affect operational performance and supply chain resilience. Evidence on the contribution of predictive analytics to both logistics optimisation and resilience is still fragmented, and opportunities exist to anticipate these risks and inform timely logistics decision-making. This systematic review aims to collate evidence on the use of predictive analytics to improve supply chain resilience and optimise logistics operations in volatile operating environments, with a specific focus on predictive techniques, applications, outcomes, and implementation challenges. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Terms relating to predictive analytics, supply chains and logistics, resilience and risk, and optimisation were used to search Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection. Eligible studies applied machine learning, deep learning, artificial intelligence (AI)-based predictive modelling, or related forecasting approaches to problems involving uncertainty, disruption, risk, resilience, or optimisation in supply-chain and/or logistics settings. After deduplication, 321 unique records were screened by title and abstract; 30 reports underwent full-text assessment, and 15 studies were included in the synthesis. Results: The 15 included studies showed substantial methodological and contextual heterogeneity. Applications concentrated on demand forecasting, inventory management, supplier risk, disruption prediction, and product availability. Methods included ensemble learning, deep learning, hybrid models, and adaptive approaches. Predictive performance often improved relative to study-specific comparators, although greater model complexity did not consistently produce better performance. The clearest operational gains were reported when predictions were coupled with optimisation or decision-support processes such as inventory allocation, replenishment, and supplier selection. Evidence relevant to resilience was strongest for anticipation, visibility, response, and recovery, whereas direct evidence for longer-term adaptation remained limited. Common implementation constraints included data quality, data availability, model adaptability, interpretability, and organisational infrastructure. Conclusion: Predictive analytics can support supply-chain resilience and logistics performance when predictive outputs are translated into timely operational decisions. The evidence remains heterogeneous and context-dependent; future research should prioritise external validation, longitudinal assessment, and direct measurement of resilience outcomes.

documents.abstract: Unaccounted-for water loss resulting from undetected underground pipe leaks poses a persistent operational and financial challenge for municipal distribution systems worldwide. In conventional utility practice, leaks are predominantly identified reactively—either when water eventually breaches the surface or following localized pressure drop complaints from consumers. In this paper, we develop a proactive, multi-sensor predictive leakage detection framework that pairs a low-power edge Internet of Things (IoT) architecture with a hybrid machine learning pipeline. Subsurface pipe segments are monitored using five complementary sensing modalities: hydraulic pressure, inline flow velocity, pipe-wall structural vibration via a MEMS accelerometer, soil moisture, and ambient temperature. Sensor readings are acquired, pre-filtered, and transmitted by an energy-efficient ESP32-based edge node using LoRa wireless communication and TLS-secured MQTT to a central analytics backend. A sliding-window feature extraction stage derives short-term statistical trends and feeds an unsupervised Isolation Forest model; the resulting anomaly metric is concatenated with temporal features to train a gradient boosting classifier that forecasts the likelihood of a leak initiating within a two-hour predictive lead window (H = 12 steps). We evaluate the proposed approach on a synthetic distribution network of 60 pipe segments that explicitly incorporates gradual, incipient mechanical degradation prior to burst onset. Benchmarked against a conventional static pressure threshold (F1 = 0.830) and standard supervised classifiers, the proposed hybrid model achieves an F1-score of 0.992 and provides a median warning lead time of 1.9 hours (mean 1.8 hours) ahead of physical rupture, with zero false alarms and zero missed events across held-out test segments. Finally, we analyze model sensitivity across noise regimes and establish key deployment requirements for district metered area field implementations.

Musculoskeletal pain (MSP) represents a major public health challenge globally, particularly among university students who are in a critical transitional phase of life characterized by intense academic demands, lifestyle changes, and increasing reliance on digital technologies. Sedentary behavior (SB) has been identified as a potential risk factor for MSP; however, evidence from the Arab region remains limited. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of MSP in nine body regions (neck, shoulders, upper back, elbows, wrists/hands, lower back, hips/thighs, knees, and ankles/feet) across four time points (lifetime, past 12 months, past month, and today), to assess the impact of MSP, and examine the association between SB and MSP. A multinational cross-sectional study was conducted among 4300 university students in seven Arab countries (Egypt, Yemen, Iraq, Sudan, Jordan, Syria, and Palestine), using an online Arabic self-administered questionnaire. Convenience and snowball sampling methods were used to recruit eligible study respondents. MSP was assessed using the Arabic version of the Extended Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ-E). SB was assessed using sedentary behavior questionnaire (SBQ). Chi-square tests were used for univariate associations. Binary logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with any MSP in the past 12 months, and to identify predictors of high SB. Adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The prevalence of MSP in at least one body region was 84.0% (lifetime), 71.3% (past 12 months), and 64.9% (past month). The neck (49.3%) and lower back (37.3%) were the most affected regions in the past 12 months. Among those affected, preventing usual activities (range: 48.8%–71.7%) and taking medication (range: 37.6–48.2%) were the most reported impacts, while hospitalization remained relatively low (3.2–14.2%). Female sex (aOR = 1.98, 95% CI 1.69–2.31), chronic diseases (aOR = 1.90, 95% CI 1.44–2.49), MSP family history (aOR = 1.96, 95% CI 1.56–2.47), moderate SB (aOR = 1.56, 95% CI 1.32–1.84), and high SB (aOR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.16–1.72) were significantly associated with MSP in the past 12 months, while sleeping 6–8 h was protective (aOR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.67–0.92). This study found a high prevalence of MSP among university students in Arab countries, particularly affecting the neck and lower back. Higher SB, chronic diseases, and a family history of MSP were associated with MSP, whereas adequate sleep appeared to be protective. These findings support the need for university-based strategies that reduce prolonged SB and promote musculoskeletal health, including ergonomic education, active breaks, adjustable study stations, and more active learning environments.

Background Low back pain (LBP) is a leading cause of disability, particularly in labor-intensive industries. While biomechanical hazards are well-documented in developed nations, epidemiological data from unregulated construction sectors in post-conflict regions remains extremely scarce. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence and identify factors associated with LBP among manual construction workers in Mogadishu, Somalia. Methods An analytic cross-sectional study was conducted among 191 manual workers recruited via stratified random sampling from five major construction companies. Data were collected using a culturally-adapted Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire to assess socio-demographic, lifestyle, and occupational exposures. We utilized a multivariable mixed-effects logistic regression model, accounting for clustering by company, to identify independent associated factors. Results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results The workforce was notably young (median age = 26 years), registering an LBP period prevalence of 51.9% (95% CI: 43.5–60.3%). In the adjusted analysis, income status was the strongest predictor, with workers living below extreme poverty facing elevated odds of LBP (AOR = 7.60; 95% CI: 2.48–23.28). Other factors significantly associated included possessing over six years of work experience (AOR = 4.85; 95% CI: 1.56–15.11), being underweight (AOR = 5.22; 95% CI: 1.24–21.94), tobacco use (AOR = 5.70; 95% CI: 1.94–16.78), and inadequate sleep duration of fewer than six hours (AOR = 4.11; 95% CI: 1.28–13.24). Biomechanically, frequency of heavy lifting (AOR = 4.29; 95% CI: 1.26–14.56) and bending (AOR = 5.35; 95% CI: 1.33–21.45) were strongly associated with reporting LBP. Conclusion LBP is highly prevalent among construction workers in Mogadishu. The factors associated with LBP were extreme poverty, inadequate physiological tissue recovery, and severe biomechanical overload. Mitigating this crisis requires site-level ergonomic interventions, such as team-lifting protocols, alongside overarching policies that establish baseline wages to address foundational socioeconomic hazards.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The expansion of Google digital services and the growing integration of generative artificial intelligence have intensified the importance of privacy, user control, and trust in digital-service relationships. This study examines whether privacy concern and perceived privacy control are associated with trust in Google digital services and whether these perceptions, together with trust, explain users’ intention to continue using Google/Gemini services in Bangladesh. Drawing on Privacy Calculus Theory and Trust Theory, the study develops a model in which privacy concern is expected to reduce trust, perceived privacy control is expected to strengthen trust, and trust is expected to increase continued-use intention. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was applied to the Group 2 Google master dataset. After screening, 385 complete cases were retained, with all retained respondents satisfying the attention-check criterion. Three-item measures captured privacy concern, perceived privacy control, trust, and continued-use intention using a five-point Likert scale. Composite-score regressions with bootstrap inference were used to reproduce the planned SEM/PLSSEM-oriented structural assessment. The results indicate that perceived privacy control positively predicts trust (β = .167, p = .001), whereas privacy concern does not have a statistically significant effect on trust (β = .080, p = .114). Trust is a substantial positive predictor of continued-use intention (β = .347, p < .001), and perceived privacy control also has a positive direct association with continued use (β = .129, p = .007). Privacy concern does not significantly predict continued use (β = .058, p = .217). Bootstrap mediation indicates a significant indirect effect of perceived privacy control through trust, while the privacy-concern indirect effect is not statistically distinguishable from zero. The findings suggest that users’ perceived ability to understand and manage privacy settings may be more consequential for trust and continued use than generalized privacy concern alone. The study contributes Bangladesh-specific evidence to privacy-calculus and trust research and offers practical implications for Google and other digital-service providers seeking to strengthen transparency, user control, and durable trust in the generative-AI era.

Introduction Sensory and spatial characteristics of learning environments can influence how neurodivergent students participate in education. This study examined professional accounts of built‐environment barriers relevant to neuro-inclusive secondary‐school design in Nigeria. Methods Seven multidisciplinary professionals were interviewed virtually using a semi‐structured guide. Four had direct experience with secondary‐school‐aged learners, while others worked in therapeutic, special‐needs, rehabilitation, or care/support settings. Open‐ended responses were analysed inductively using reflexive thematic analysis, while responses to nine predefined design features were synthesised separately as prompted feature appraisals. Results Four themes were generated: sensory environmental stressors; environmental distress and spatial dysregulation; restorative and regulatory features; and spatial configuration, transition, and classroom ergonomics. Auditory and visual conditions, crowding, abrupt transitions, and limited retreat space were prominent concerns. Funding, space, institutional readiness, and implementation knowledge affected feasibility. A preliminary three‐tier retrofit framework prioritised acoustic control, lighting control, withdrawal/escape spaces, and sensory zoning (Tier 1); flexible furniture and wayfinding/predictability (Tier 2); and biophilic respite, visual simplification/colour, and temperature/ventilation (Tier 3). Discussion The findings provide mixed‐context professional proxy evidence relevant to Nigerian secondary‐school design. The framework is preliminary and unvalidated and should be tested through co‐design with neurodivergent students and objective environmental assessment.

This chapter, per the authors, examines RAISE-STEM as a translational framework for human-centered artificial intelligence design in higher education. It responds to the gap between instrumental AI adoption and the broader sociotechnical challenges of agency, equity, data ethics, governance, and inclusive learning design. Drawing on sociotechnical theory, Actor-Network perspectives, and governance-oriented AI scholarship, the chapter reconceptualizes the five RAISE-STEM dimensions as mechanisms that connect classroom-level pedagogical change with institutional and ecosystem-level design. The chapter analyzes how macro, meso, and micro governance levels must operate coherently to support ethical, equitable, and pedagogically meaningful AI integration. It also introduces a Translational Design Architecture that maps each RAISE-STEM dimension to its human-centered design logic, governance level, key risk, and evaluation criterionwith a research agenda for participatory governance and empirical validation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Increasingly realistic generative AI has made manipulated video, audio, and text a viable threat to digital trustworthiness.This paper describes a proposed Real-Time Multimedia Deepfake Analyzer that fuses visual, acoustic, and linguistic evidence into a single server-based decision-support workflow.The analyzer processes localized facial geometry and spatial-temporal changes, acoustic features extracted from mel-spectrograms and vocal cadence, and speech transcripts which may include regional Indian languages or code-switched dialogue.An intermediate crossmodal fusion layer evaluates phoneme-viseme synchronization, audio-visual consistency, and semantic alignment while compression augmentation is included to improve resistance to media circulated via messaging and social platforms.A Flask-based web interface for displaying authenticity scores, real/fake decisions, and evidencelocalization cues to aid human review is described, utilizing PyTorch and OpenCV for model and vision processing.The design emphasizes explainability, deployment practicality, and evaluation on both clean and degraded media.As this synopsis describes a proposed system and evaluation methodology rather than experimental results, this paper presents the architecture and validation methodology without making claims regarding measured detection performance.

The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into modern higher education has produced a dual impact: while AI has opened new opportunities for innovation in teaching, learning, and research, it has also introduced significant challenges for academic practice. This paper explores how AI reshapes epistemic boundaries by challenging traditional notions and examines how confidence in institutional traditions and technological promise intersects with empirical data and algorithmic reasoning, and the ethical implications for transparent decision-making frameworks. By combining theoretical perspectives with practical examples, this paper highlights how AI is redefining epistemological foundations by the need to strengthen the relationship between faith and facts. The paper argues for a human-centred approach that promotes adaptive learning cultures. It concludes by proposing a forward-looking framework to help modern universities remain grounded in an AI-intensive future.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The development of information technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) has shifted the paradigm of state resilience away from protection oriented toward territorial areas and toward the protection of a borderless digital space. This shift presents new challenges for the state in protecting its citizens, as reflected in the cyberattack on Indonesia's Temporary National Data Center (PDNS) in 2024. Although Indonesia already has various regulations concerning information technology, cybersecurity, and personal data protection, national legal policy has not yet been fully able to build an integrated framework to respond to digital threats in the AI era. This research aims to analyze the legal policy of state resilience in protecting citizens through a case study of the cyberattack on PDNS, and to reconstruct legal policy based on Digital Sovereignty as a paradigm for strengthening state resilience. This research uses the normative legal research method with statutory, conceptual, and case approaches. The results show that the national legal framework remains sectoral in nature and has not been able to comprehensively integrate cybersecurity governance, data protection, and the use of AI. Therefore, this research offers a reconstruction of legal policy based on Digital Sovereignty, which places control over data, digital infrastructure, cybersecurity, and AI governance as a new foundation for strengthening state resilience while guaranteeing the protection of citizens' constitutional rights in the era of digital transformation. The proposed model integrates data sovereignty, infrastructure resilience, AI accountability, supply chain security, and digital human capacity through preventive, adaptive, rights based governance mechanisms for public institutions.

documents.abstract: Abstract Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. By monolithically integrating optical delay lines and crossings within segmented slow-light phase shifters, we synthesized an on-chip feedforward response that extends the 3-dB bandwidth. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems.

Ayurvedic Dravya identification is an important process in Ayurveda, as the correct identification of medicinal substances supports their appropriate use and quality assessment. However, identifying Ayurvedic Dravya based on sensory characteristics such as Rasa (taste) can be challenging because different substances may exhibit similar taste profiles, while their responses can vary with sample concentration, solvent composition and preparation conditions. Traditional sensory evaluation also depends on human perception and may introduce subjectivity. An electronic tongue (E-tongue), which uses an array of chemical sensors to generate measurable response patterns, offers a potential approach for objective and repeatable taste-related analysis. This paper proposes a Reference-Anchored Multi-Dilution Electronic Tongue framework for Ayurvedic Dravya identification. The proposed system evaluates each sample at multiple predefined dilution levels to obtain a more representative sensor-response fingerprint. The collected signals are preprocessed, normalised and compared with reference fingerprints stored in a database using a deterministic distancebased matching method. Unlike approaches that depend on artificial intelligence or machine-learning classification, the proposed framework focuses on reference-based comparison, controlled sample preparation, sensor calibration and predefined acceptance criteria. The system is designed to provide the closest reference match when the similarity criteria are satisfied and a “No Reliable Match” result when the evidence is insufficient. The paper also discusses key challenges, including sensor drift, variation in sample composition, solvent effects, dilution consistency and the need for laboratory reference validation. The proposed framework may support the development of a transparent and reproducible electronic-tongue system for Ayurvedic Dravya screening. Experimental validation with authenticated samples is required to establish its identification performance, repeatability and practical suitability.

Posthumanism has become an important critical framework for rethinking the boundaries of the human in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, biotechnology, ecological crisis, and complex human–nonhuman relations. Earlier versions of this study offered a broad theoretical survey of posthumanist thinkers, but a research article requires a more clearly delimited corpus, method, research problem, and analytical findings.

The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in learning mathematics among fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05. This study was motivated by the increasing use of generative AI as a learning tool and the low level of students’ interest in mathematics. A quantitative approach with a correlational survey design was employed. The population consisted of all fifth-grade students at SDN Kebalen 05, and a saturated sampling technique was used. Data were collected primarily through questionnaires, with observations, documentation, and interviews serving as supporting data. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson Product-Moment correlation analysis. The results showed a strong positive relationship between the use of generative AI, represented by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and students’ interest in mathematics learning (r = 0.682, p < 0.001). This finding indicates that higher use of generative AI was associated with higher interest in mathematics learning among fifth-grade students. The findings suggest that the appropriate use of generative AI may provide teachers with complementary tools for creating more interactive mathematics learning experiences and may be considered in supporting students’ learning interest. The study provides practical implications for teachers in integrating AI-based learning tools appropriately as complementary resources in primary mathematics education.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly incorporated into journalistic work, raising questions concerning transparency, authorship, editorial responsibility, human verification, and organizational governance. This study examines reported transparency practices and professional perceptions concerning AI use among journalism professionals linked to media organizations and news-production environments in Ecuador. A mixed-methods design combined a non-probability online survey of 53 eligible professionals with seven semi-structured interviews involving six journalism professionals and one communication academic with professional experience in journalism. The quantitative component was analyzed descriptively, while the qualitative component was examined through a deductive and interpretive analysis structured around four predefined thematic domains. AI use was reported by 48 of the 53 survey participants (90.6%), with both instrumental and generative applications identified. Among applicable responses, 39.5% reported the existence of a specific AI-related deontological code, 59.2% reported having received instructions from superiors, and 29.3% reported an obligation to disclose AI use to audiences. Human verification was the most frequently selected component of proposed internal AI rules (79.2%). The interviews showed uneven levels of organizational formalization, including verbal instructions, emerging guidelines, and differing thresholds for disclosure, while consistently emphasizing human editorial judgment and responsibility. The findings indicate that transparency in AI-assisted journalism is multidimensional and unevenly institutionalized across the professional environments represented in the study. These results provide sample-bound evidence from Ecuador and should not be interpreted as a national estimate of media transparency.
